Abstract:
This article concerns anisotropy in stress–strain relationships exhibited by steel pipelines. Since the stress from internal pressurization is highest in the hoop direction, standard industrial practice to measure these properties has focussed on tensile testing in this direction, requiring a prior flattening operation. The associated plastic deformation may affect properties, typically causing a (poorly‐defined) degree of hardening and the creation of inhomogeneity. Field testing of such pipelines, requiring in situ measurement of tensile properties (yield stress (YS) and ultimate tensile stress (UTS)), is based on indentation testing of the outer surface. One such test (profilometry‐based indentation plastometry (PIP)), not only gives the stress–strain curve, but also allows detection of any (in‐plane) anisotropy, with a high sensitivity. Both PIP testing and compression testing (with and without prior flattening) have confirmed that none of the eight pipes examined in the current work exhibited any such anisotropy, although the effects of flattening did tend to generate apparent anisotropy in the tensile test outcomes. It may therefore be appropriate to switch the focus of tensile testing to the axial direction, such that no flattening would be required.

Abstract:
Herein, the flattening and subsequent tensile testing (in the hoop direction) of steel pipes used for transmission of oil and gas are concerned. A particular focus is on the use of a novel indentation plastometry test (PIP), applied to the outer free surface of an as‐received pipe. This allows a stress–strain curve to be obtained from a relatively small volume (a disk of diameter about 1 mm and thickness around 100–200 μm). Whole section and reduced section tensile testing, of as‐received and flattened samples are carried out. Four different pipes are studied. While there are some variations between them, there is a general trend for near‐surface regions of the pipe to be a little harder than the interior, and for flattened pipes to be a little harder than unflattened ones, although these are not dramatic or well‐defined effects. PIP testing also confirms that these pipes exhibit little or no anisotropy. It is in general concluded that PIP‐derived stress–strain curves for testing of the outside of a pipe are likely to be quite close to those obtained by tensile testing of the whole section in the hoop direction, after flattening.

Abstract:
Herein, it is concerned with the use of profilometry‐based indentation plastometry (PIP) to obtain mechanical property information for particulate metal matrix composites (MMCs). This type of test, together with conventional uniaxial testing, has been applied to four different MMCs (produced with various particulate contents and processing conditions). It is shown that reliable stress–strain curves can be obtained using PIP, although the possibility of premature (prenecking) fracture should be noted. Close attention is paid to scale effects. As a consequence of variations in local spatial distributions of particulate, the “representative volume” of these materials can be relatively large. This can lead to a certain amount of scatter in PIP profiles and it is advisable to carry out a number of repeat PIP tests in order to obtain macroscopic properties. Nevertheless, it is shown that PIP testing can reliably detect the relatively minor (macroscopic) anisotropy exhibited by forged materials of this type.

Abstract:
Integrating machine learning into additive manufacturing offers transformative opportunities to optimize material properties and design high-performance, fatigue-resistant structures for critical applications in aerospace, biomedical, and structural engineering. This study explores mechanistic machine learning techniques to tailor microstructural features, leveraging data from ultrasonic fatigue tests where very high cycle fatigue properties were assessed up to 1×1010 cycles. Machine learning models predicted critical fatigue thresholds, optimized process parameters, and reduced design iteration cycles by over 50%, leading to faster production of safer, more durable components. By refining grain orientation and phase uniformity, fatigue crack propagation resistance improved by 20–30%, significantly enhancing fatigue life and reliability for mission-critical aerospace components, such as turbine blades and structural airframe parts, in an industry where failure is not an option. Additionally, the machine learning-driven design of metamaterials enabled structures with a 15% weight reduction and improved yield strength, demonstrating the feasibility of bioinspired geometries for lightweight applications in space exploration, medical implants, and high-performance automotive components. In the area of titanium and aluminum alloys, machine learning identified key process parameters such as temperature gradients and cooling rates, which govern microstructural evolution and enable fatigue-resistant designs tailored for high-stress environments in aircraft, biomedical prosthetics, and high-speed transportation. Combining theoretical insights and experimental validations, this research highlights the potential of machine learning to refine microstructural properties and establish intelligent, adaptive manufacturing systems, ensuring enhanced reliability, performance, and efficiency in cutting-edge engineering applications.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing of aluminum (Al) alloys has attracted significant attention in the aerospace industry. However, achieving ultrahigh-strength (>500 MPa) Al alloys remains challenging due to their intrinsic poor printability. Here, we report a novel hybrid additive manufacturing (HAM) approach to process ultrahigh-strength AlMgSc alloy, which combines laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with interlayer ultrasonic shot peening (USP). The results show that the interlayer ultrasonic shot peening depth reached ∼700 µm, leading to almost full density and residual stress convection from tension to compression. The HAM method promotes equiaxed grain formation and refines grain due to grain recrystallizations. Interestingly, the HAM followed by aging treatment tailors the hierarchically multi-gradient structures, inhibits Mg element intragranular segregation, and promotes the multi-nanoprecipitates (e.g. Al3(Sc, Zr) and Al6Mn) precipitation. Remarkably, the HAM followed by aging treatment achieves yield strength of 609 MPa and breaks elongation of 7.5%, demonstrating ultrahigh strength and good ductility compared with other Al alloys manufactured by AM and forging as reported in the literature. The strength enhancement mechanisms in this AlMgSc alloy are discussed. The high-density Al3(Sc, Zr) precipitates are the main strengthening contributor, and unique hetero-deformation induced (HDI) strengthening (originates from the heterogeneous microstructures) further enhances the strength of the material. This work highlights a novel approach for processing complex-structured ultrahigh strength Al alloy components by hybrid additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
As the fatigue properties of as-built components of additively manufactured (AM) metals are considerably weaker than those of wrought metals because of their rougher surface, post-processing is necessary to improve the fatigue properties. To demonstrate the improvement in the fatigue properties of AM metals via post-processing methods, the fabrication of AlSi10Mg, i.e., PBF–LS/AlSi10Mg, through powder bed fusion (PBF) using laser sintering (LS) and its treatment via submerged laser peening (SLP), using a fiber laser and/or a Nd/YAG laser, was evaluated via plane bending fatigue tests. In SLP, laser ablation (LA) is generated by a pulsed laser and a bubble is generated after LA, which behaves like a cavitation bubble that is referred to as “laser cavitation (LC)”. In this paper, LA-dominated SLP is referred to as “laser treatment (LT)”, while LC collapse-dominated SLP is referred to as “laser cavitation peening (LCP)”, as the impact of LC collapse is used for peening. It was revealed that SLP using a fiber laser corresponded with LT rather than LCP. It was demonstrated that the fatigue strength at N = 107 was 85 MPa for LCP and 103 MPa for the combined process of blasting (B) + LT + LCP, whereas the fatigue strength of the as-built specimen was 54 MPa.

Abstract:
This paper investigates the tear resistance of three cast and homogenized 6000-series alloys, namely AA6061, AA6063 and AA6110, all in temper T6, by means of Kahn tear tests. Of each alloy one commercial version and one tailor-made version were studied. The tailor-made alloys were designed to have approximately three times higher content of constituent particles by increasing the amount of Fe and Si in the chemical composition. The aim was to study in what way a higher constituent-particle content affects the tear resistance and properties of the alloys. The research showed that the unit initiation and propagation energies measured from the Kahn tear tests are markedly reduced when the constituent-particle content is increased, and that the tear resistance is reduced by a higher fraction than the failure strain of the smooth tensile tests. No major differences in the fracture mode and the fracture mechanisms between the alloys with normal and with high constituent-particle content were revealed by the use of computed tomography scanning or scanning electron microscopy imaging. It was concluded for the alloys studied that the increased content of constituent particles had a significant effect on the tear resistance, while the fracture mode and mechanisms remained the same.

Abstract:
The determination of the material parameters that best predict the local ductility of high strength sheet materials has become the focus of active research. Even though several correlations have been proposed, they can sometimes be not accurate enough and discussion is still open on this topic. This paper investigates the suitability of different fracture toughness measurements for local ductility prediction in multiple advanced high strength steels (AHSS). Fracture toughness is characterized by means of essential work of fracture and Khan tear tests. The results show that the essential work of fracture, we, correlates well with different local formability (HER, critical bending angle from V-bending tests and local strain at fracture from uniaxial tensile tests) and crash resistance parameters (energy absorbed in axial impact tests). It confirms that fracture toughness, measured in the frame of fracture mechanics, is a relevant material property to rationalize cracking issues associated to the local ductility of AHSS. On the other hand, it is also shown that Khan tear tests, which are conventionally used to evaluate the fracture resistance of thin metal sheets, can overestimate crack propagation resistance and offer a poor prediction ability for local formability and crash performance.

Abstract:
The deformation aspects associated with the micro-mechanical properties of the powder laser bed fusion (P-LBF) additively manufactured stainless steel 316L were investigated in the present work. Toward that, micro-pillars were fabricated on different planes of the stainless steel 316L specimen with respect to build direction, and an in situ compression was carried out inside the chamber of the scanning electron microscope (SEM). The results were compared against the compositionally similar stainless steel 316L, which was fabricated by a conventional method, that is, casting. The post-deformed micro-pillars on the both materials were examined by electron microscopy. The P-LBF processed steel exhibits equiaxed as well as elongated grains of different orientation with the characteristics of the melt-pool type arrangements. In contrast, the cast alloy shows typical circular-type grains in the presence of micro-twins. The yield stress and ultimate compressive stress of P-LBF fabricated steel were about 431.02 ± 15.51 − 474.44 ± 23.49 MPa and 547.78 ± 29.58 − 682.59 ± 21.59 MPa, respectively. Whereas for the cast alloy, it was about 322.38 ± 19.78 MPa and 477.11 ± 25.31 MPa, respectively. Thus, the outcome of this study signifies that the AM-processed samples possess higher mechanical properties than conventionally processed alloy of similar composition. Irrespective of the processing method, both specimens exhibit ductile-type deformation, which is typical for metallic alloys.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing offers precise control over part geometry and material composition, making it ideal for creating functionally integrated materials (FIMs). A Ni-Al FIM was fabricated using directed energy deposition (DED) to investigate how local composition variations affect microstructure, precipitation, and mechanical behavior. Advanced microscopy characterization revealed a novel grain structure with distinct compositional regions and a composition transition interface. These distinct regions within a single grain led to abrupt changes in the deformation response, as demonstrated through in-situ micropillar compression. These findings underscore the potential of additive manufacturing to engineer material behavior at the microscale, advancing materials design and manufacturing. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT IMPACT STATEMENT Towards additive manufacturing of functionally integrated materials, this study explores a novel approach to engineering the microstructure and mechanical behavior via spatial control of alloy composition within a single grain.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A micropillar compression study with two different techniques was performed on proton-irradiated additively manufactured (AM) 316L stainless steels. The sample was irradiated at 360 °C using 2 MeV protons to 1.8 average displacement per atom (dpa) in the near-surface region. A comparison study with mechanical test and microstructure characterization was made between planar and cross-sectional pillars prepared from the irradiated surface. While a 2 MeV proton irradiation creates a relatively flat damage zone up to 12 µm, the dpa gradient by a factor of 2 leads to significant dpa uncertainty along the pillar height direction for the conventional planar technique. Cross-sectional pillars can significantly reduce such dpa uncertainty. From one single sample, three cross-sectional pillars were able to show dpa-dependent hardening. Furthermore, post-compression transmission electron microscopy allows the determination of the deformation mechanism of individual micropillars. Cross-sectional micropillar compression can be used to study radiation-induced mechanical property changes with better resolution and less data fluctuation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
To investigate the mechanical properties of electron beam melted (EBM) Ti-6Al-4V alloy at the microscale, a series of in situ scanning electron microscope (SEM) compression experiments were performed in the current study. Firstly, a reconstruction of the original β phase of Ti-6Al-4V alloy was conducted using electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) analysis. Micro-pillars were subsequently fabricated with a diameter of 2 μm within the same original β phase grain, and yield strength was measured using an in-situ mechanical compression device. ## pqac-00000019

From text 'sekhar2018hardnessyield pages 3-6'.

Aluru Praveen Sekhar, Supriya Nandy, Kalyan Kumar Ray, and Debdulal Das. Hardness - yield strength relation of al-mg-si alloys. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering, 338:012011, Mar 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899x/338/1/012011, doi:10.1088/1757-899x/338/1/012011. This article has 37 citations.

The excerpt supports a useful but alloy- and condition-dependent relationship between Vickers hardness and yield strength in aluminum alloys. Tabor’s model relates mean indentation pressure to yield strength through the constraint factor: Pm ≈ 2.956σys for the Vickers geometry, with HV = 0.927Pm. Combining these gives σys = HV/(0.927C). For fully work-hardened materials and C = 2.956, the expected hardness–yield-strength slope is about 0.365, with an intercept of zero; this is the classic Tabor relation. For strain-hardening and age-hardenable Al-Mg-Si alloys, however, a linear equation with a fitted intercept is more appropriate. In the selected alloy, regression produced R² = 0.937, and a constrained fit was σys = 0.383HV − 101.5 (with hardness and strength units consistent with the paper). Literature data for A356, A357, AA6061, and AA6063 also showed good linear Vickers-hardness/yield-strength relationships, although prior Brinell correlations for A356/A357 exhibited significant scatter. Important limitations are that the constraint factor depends on indenter geometry and material behavior, the zero-intercept Tabor assumption may fail, and aging state, strain hardening, precipitate evolution, and experimental or literature differences affect the correlation. The excerpt provides no direct evidence for Rockwell or nanoindentation-based predictions.

The excerpt evaluates hardness–yield-strength prediction primarily for Vickers hardness (HV) in age-hardenable Al–Mg–Si alloys; it does not provide comparable evidence for Rockwell, Brinell, or nanoindentation. Linear regressions vary substantially by alloy and dataset. Reported R² values range from 0.767 to 0.991, indicating that hardness can be a useful predictor within a consistent alloy, processing, and temper condition, but its accuracy is not universal. For the present alloy, the fitted relationship has a slope of 0.383 and a negative intercept of 101.5 (in the relevant stress/hardness units). Validation against experimental and literature data shows most predictions within 15%–30% error bands, while outliers involve differing solution treatments, quenching conditions, highly over-aged states, or differently homogenized samples. The Tabor framework relates flow stress to hardness; for fully work-hardened material, the excerpt gives σf = HV/(0.927C), with σf equated to yield strength. For strain-hardened materials, indentation produces a representative strain and σf exceeds σys, giving the modified relation σys = HV/(0.927C) − Δσ. Thus, the negative intercept reflects indentation-induced strain hardening. Correlations are limited by alloy chemistry, heat treatment, microstructure, strain-hardening behavior, and testing condition consistency.

The excerpt supports the usual Tabor-style interpretation of hardness: in the fully plastic regime, mean contact pressure (or indentation hardness) is approximately a constraint factor of about 3 times the representative flow or yield stress. Thus, an estimated lower yield strength can be obtained by dividing the true mean contact pressure by approximately 3. In this aluminum alloy, the resulting nanoindentation lower-yield estimate was reasonably comparable to the bulk tensile 0.2% yield strength of about 0.32 GPa. However, the comparison is conditional rather than universal. Nanoindentation probes a localized volume and can show size-dependent strengthening, delayed plasticity, and abrupt pop-in; the pre-pop-in stress may be much higher than the bulk tensile yield strength. Hardness also reflects plastic flow and strain hardening, not necessarily a uniquely defined tensile yield point. If the alloy does not strain-harden, pile-up causes the standard contact-depth analysis to underestimate contact area and overestimate mean pressure; the excerpt notes errors of up to about 60% for pyramidal indenters and potentially more for spherical ones. Consequently, hardness-to-yield correlations depend on indenter geometry, constraint factor, contact-area calibration, pile-up/sink-in, strain-hardening behavior, microstructure, surface condition, and indentation size/length scale. ## pqac-00000042

From text 'zhao2006exfoliationcorrosionkinetics pages 80-90'.

X Zhao. Exfoliation corrosion kinetics of high strength aluminum alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt directly addresses ASTM G34 exfoliation testing but does not provide the requested ASTM G47 or G139 stress-corrosion-cracking procedures, specimen dimensions, exposure temperatures, solution compositions, or test durations. It explains that exfoliation corrosion is an intergranular attack associated particularly with wrought aluminum alloys having elongated grain structures. Intergranular attack parallel to the surface produces hydrated aluminum oxide whose volume exceeds that of the original alloy, generating wedging stresses that lift surface grains and create the characteristic layered appearance. ASTM G34 (the EXCO test) assesses exfoliation susceptibility by exposing specimens to an oxidizing acidic chloride solution and comparing the resulting surface with standard photographs. The excerpt also mentions ASSET and MASTMAASIS tests, which use alternating salt-solution sprays and surface ratings. These tests are important for aerospace applications because exfoliation is a life-limiting airframe degradation mechanism: it removes load-bearing cross-sectional area and raises stresses in the remaining intact material, reducing mechanical properties. The passage therefore supports the purpose and significance of G34, but additional source material is required to specify G47/G139 testing and the exact G34 specimen and exposure requirements.

## pqac-00000043

From text 'zhao2006exfoliationcorrosionkinetics pages 39-43'.

The excerpt directly addresses ASTM G34 exfoliation testing, but it does not provide information on ASTM G47 or G139 stress-corrosion-cracking tests, including their specimen requirements, temperatures, solutions, or exposure durations. For G34, the EXCO immersion test evaluates exfoliation susceptibility in principally 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys. It uses an aggressive solution containing 4.0 M NaCl, 0.5 M KNO3, and 0.1 M HNO3, initially at pH 0.4. Specimens are immersed continuously for approximately 48–96 hours, depending on alloy system, and the surface is visually rated from N (no appreciable attack) and P (pitting) through EA–ED degrees of exfoliation. The test can distinguish resistant and susceptible tempers, such as AA7075-T76 and AA7075-T6, and has correlated with atmospheric exposure for some alloys. However, it may overstate attack, fail to reproduce service environments, and correlate poorly for some Al-Li, AA2024, and 7x50 products. Modified EXCO solutions can improve correlation with actual service. These tests are important for aerospace aluminum because they identify susceptibility in lightweight, high-strength alloys before service, supporting temper selection, quality control, and prediction of durability in humid, salt-containing marine or industrial environments. The excerpt does not state specimen dimensions or temperature.

Stress-corrosion-cracking tests reveal whether an aluminum alloy, under sustained tensile stress in a critical corrosive environment, initiates and propagates intergranular or transgranular cracks. SCC requires the simultaneous presence of a susceptible alloy, an aggressive environment, and tensile stress; crack initiation may occur at pits, surface discontinuities, or intergranular-corrosion sites. The discussion identifies anodic dissolution along active grain-boundary paths and hydrogen embrittlement as the two principal SCC propagation categories. Exfoliation testing evaluates susceptibility to layered, grain-boundary corrosion and material delamination; the excerpt specifically notes that IGSCC is one proposed mechanism of exfoliation corrosion. Microstructure is central: precipitate-free zones parallel to grain boundaries can be anodic and increase intergranular-corrosion susceptibility, while alloy particles and grain-boundary precipitates influence localized corrosion. These tests are important for aerospace aluminum because high-strength, age-hardenable alloys may retain adequate mechanical strength yet fail prematurely through localized corrosion, SCC, or exfoliation in service. Standardized exposures therefore support alloy, temper, heat-treatment, and maintenance qualification, although the cited excerpt alone cannot specify the ASTM procedures.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adem.202101398, doi:10.1002/adem.202101398. This article has 34 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) extracts a bulk true stress–true strain curve from a spherical indentation. A ball is pressed into the specimen to a selected depth, the three-dimensional residual indent profile is measured by profilometry, and an inverse finite-element procedure iteratively adjusts the constitutive stress–strain curve until the simulated and measured profiles agree. For very hard metals, the indenter must remain elastic; silicon-nitride balls can be used, with proof-testing proposed to verify that a particular ball survives the full service range. Bulk measurements require a sufficiently large, representative many-grained volume rather than a nanoscale indentation, typically using a 0.5–1 mm ball and kilonewton-capable loading frame. The excerpt reports systematic agreement with tensile and compressive tests and describes the resulting curves as reliable, including for hard metals. It specifically highlights PIP’s usefulness at relatively high strains (about 15%) and its simpler implementation compared with uniaxial testing. The excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy values for yield stress or work-hardening parameters. It indicates applicability to thin plasma-sprayed layers and anisotropic additively manufactured materials, suggesting an advantage where conventional tensile specimens are difficult to produce, but does not quantify AM-specific accuracy or benefits.

Consequently, applying conventional MMPDS qualification directly to additive manufacturing would be expensive, time-consuming, and potentially of limited long-term meaning. The excerpt explains that MMPDS provides statistically guaranteed minimum material properties rather than relying on typical values. For conventional metals, A-basis and B-basis are the established allowables. For additive manufacturing, equivalent terminology is used because AM properties vary with build direction, build-plate location, machine, and software version: C-basis is the AM equivalent of A-basis, while D-basis is the equivalent of B-basis. The stated requirements are that C-basis is a minimum value exceeded by at least 99% of the population with 95% confidence, whereas D-basis is exceeded by at least 90% with 95% confidence. The excerpt does not provide a fixed specimen count for either allowable. It emphasizes that establishing a C-basis for one AM material–process combination may require testing hundreds of coupons across multiple machines and build batches. Thus, AM qualification must account for process and configuration variability rather than treating one dataset as universally applicable. The large physical-testing burden motivates validated physics-informed and computational models, including virtual coupon testing, to predict properties and reduce the number of required specimens while retaining statistically defensible qualification. --- ## pqac-00000073 From text 'abdi2020materialallowablegeneration pages 9-11'. The excerpt describes MMPDS-style A- and B-basis allowables for additive-manufactured materials. An A-basis allowable is a conservative design value for which at least 99% of the material-strength population is expected to meet or exceed the value, with 95% confidence. A B-basis allowable requires 90% of the population to meet or exceed the value; the excerpt does not explicitly repeat the 95% confidence statement for B-basis, although the question supplies that criterion. B-basis values are intended for redundant structures in which failure of one element permits safe load redistribution. For full A- or B-basis determination, the cited plan calls for 100 tensile specimens drawn from 10 heats and 10 lots. If tensile allowables have already been established, only 20 specimens are needed for properties such as shear and compression allowables. A reduced B-basis plan uses 20 samples from three heats and reduced lots. For additive-manufacturing qualification, the process should establish a generic acceptance region across different batches, machines, and process conditions, then use it for qualification, proto-qualification, acceptance, and validation. Qualification may rely on extensive testing, reduced/equivalence-based testing, or model-based simulation. A B-basis allowable (T90) similarly requires at least 90% of the population to meet or exceed the value, also with 95% confidence. Allowables are calculated from the sample mean, standard deviation, and a derating/tolerance factor; that factor depends on the assumed distribution, sample size (degrees of freedom), desired coverage, and confidence level. The excerpt illustrates calculations using samples of 100, but this is an example, not a stated MMPDS minimum. The appropriate number of specimens therefore depends on the governing MMPDS procedure, distributional assumptions, test design, and required reliability; it cannot be determined from this excerpt alone. {"answer": "# Mechanical Tests Beyond Uniaxial Tension for Aerospace Aluminum Alloys and Additively Manufactured Metal Parts

## 1. Fracture Toughness Testing

### ASTM E399 / B645 / B646 — Plane-Strain Fracture Toughness (K_IC)

Fracture toughness testing measures resistance to crack extension under plane-strain, linear-elastic conditions, expressed as the critical stress-intensity factor K_IC. A tensile test provides yield strength, UTS, and elongation on smooth specimens but reveals nothing about how a material behaves in the presence of a pre-existing flaw. ASTM E399 requires fatigue-precracked compact-tension C(T) or single-edge-bend SE(B) specimens with specific a/W and W/B proportions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002). ASTM B645 and B646 provide practice for determining and preparing aluminum-alloy fracture-toughness specimens, respectively. For an A413 aluminum alloy with σ_YS = 82 MPa, the calculated minimum valid specimen thickness was approximately 38 mm; at σ_YS = 130 MPa, minimum thickness was approximately 18 mm (pqac-00000001). C(T) specimens of 25 mm thickness have been used for aircraft-grade 2xxx and 7xxx alloys, tested in both L-T and T-L orientations at room temperature and 219.15 K (−54 °C), with at least three specimens per orientation (pqac-00000003). These tests are time-consuming due to the fatigue pre-cracking requirement and can consume substantial material, particularly for high-toughness, low-strength alloys where validity requirements demand large specimens.

**What it reveals that tensile cannot:** Crack-initiation resistance, stable crack-growth resistance, plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC, and damage-tolerance behavior in the presence of flaws (pqac-00000002). **Strongly supported.**

### ASTM E1820 — J-Integral and CTOD

ASTM E1820 extends fracture characterization into the elastic-plastic regime via J-integral (J_IC) and crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD), applicable when plane-strain validity per E399 is not achievable. This is particularly relevant for tough aluminum alloys where valid K_IC specimens would be impractically large. J_IC testing is described as more suitable than K_IC for many aluminum alloys but experimentally more complicated (pqac-00000007).

### ASTM E561 — R-Curve (Crack-Resistance Curve)

E561 R-curve testing measures crack-resistance as a function of crack extension, capturing stable tearing behavior. This is essential for damage-tolerant design of aircraft structures where cracks may grow stably before catastrophic failure. R-curve methods can be more costly and time-consuming than tear tests (pqac-00000000). **Moderately supported** — specific procedural details from R-curve studies were not directly extracted.

### ASTM B871 — Kahn Tear Test

The Kahn tear test is an energy-based fracture test specifically developed for aluminum alloy sheet and thin products. It uses a small, V-notched specimen (typically 35 mm × 60 mm × sheet thickness, with a 60° notch and notch-root radius < 60 μm) loaded statically until a crack propagates across the specimen width (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005). For AA2139-T8 (3.2-mm sheet), specimens were 35 mm × 60 mm × 3.2 mm, with cracks arrested at ~10 mm propagation (pqac-00000005). The test measures:
- **Unit initiation energy (UE_i):** energy to initiate a crack (e.g., 79 N·mm⁻¹ in T-L and 104 N·mm⁻¹ in L-T for AA2139-T8) (pqac-00000005)
- **Unit propagation energy (UE_p):** energy for stable crack growth, identified as the representative tear-toughness measure (pqac-00000007)
- **Tear-strength-to-yield-strength ratio (TYR)** (pqac-00000000)

**Key advantage:** Low material consumption, low cost, short preparation time, and no fatigue pre-crack required (pqac-00000000). The reduction in Kahn tear resistance with increased constituent-particle content was shown to be greater than the reduction in smooth-tensile failure strain for 6xxx alloys, demonstrating that tensile ductility alone cannot predict tearing resistance (pqac-00000004). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 2. Fatigue Testing

### High-Cycle Fatigue (HCF) — ASTM E466

ASTM E466 covers force-controlled, constant-amplitude axial fatigue testing of unnotched metallic specimens, typically using round uniform-gauge or hourglass specimens. Tests are run at frequencies of 10–60 Hz (commonly ~40 Hz), with stress ratios R = −1, 0.1, or 0.5 (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). Run-outs are typically defined at 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles. For LPBF Al2024-RAM2, as-built fatigue limits at 2 × 10⁶ cycles ranged from 109 MPa (45° orientation, Ra = 17.6 μm) to 118 MPa (A-orientation, Ra = 2.1 μm); grinding to Ra = 0.6 μm raised the fatigue limit to 200 MPa (pqac-00000052). Generating a full S-N curve typically requires 15–30 specimens across multiple stress levels and takes days to weeks depending on frequency and target life.

**What it reveals that tensile cannot:** Endurance limits, S-N behavior, crack-initiation sites, and the dominant role of surface roughness and defects under cyclic loading (pqac-00000008). **Strongly supported.**

### Low-Cycle Fatigue (LCF) — ASTM E606

ASTM E606 covers strain-controlled fatigue testing at high strain amplitudes and low cycle counts (typically < 10⁴ cycles). It uses cylindrical specimens with extensometers, tested at strain rates of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹. LCF reveals cyclic stress-strain behavior, cyclic hardening/softening, hysteresis-loop evolution, and fatigue-life under plastic-strain-dominated conditions. For LPBF metals, LCF behavior depends on microstructure and strength in addition to surface and porosity effects (pqac-00000056).

### Ultrasonic Fatigue at 20 kHz

Ultrasonic fatigue testing accelerates very-high-cycle fatigue (VHCF) testing by operating at ~20 kHz, enabling exploration of fatigue behavior up to 10⁹–10¹⁰ cycles. At 20 kHz continuous loading, 10⁹ cycles can be reached in approximately 14 hours, versus months at conventional frequencies (pqac-00000008 context from Awd 2025, doi:10.3390/ma18071472). This reveals subsurface crack-initiation mechanisms, "fish-eye" fracture origins at internal defects, and the existence (or absence) of a true fatigue limit in the VHCF regime. **Moderately supported** — specific LPBF aluminum VHCF data were referenced but not directly extracted.

### Fatigue Crack Growth (FCG) — ASTM E647

ASTM E647 measures da/dN versus ΔK using pre-cracked C(T) or M(T) specimens. It reveals crack-growth rates, threshold stress-intensity factor range (ΔK_th), Paris-law constants, and the influence of R-ratio, environment, and microstructure on crack propagation. For LPBF Inconel 718, threshold ΔK values of 2–6 MPa√m were calculated from near-surface defects ~50 μm in diameter that initiated fatigue cracks (pqac-00000014). FCG testing typically requires C(T) specimens ≥ 25 mm wide and several weeks of testing per specimen.

---

## 3. Charpy Impact Testing (ASTM E23) and Why It Is Little Used for Aluminum

ASTM E23 uses a standard 10 × 10 × 55 mm notched bar struck by a pendulum to measure absorbed energy. For steels, Charpy testing is essential for identifying ductile-to-brittle transition temperatures (DBTT). Aluminum alloys, however, have FCC crystal structures that do not exhibit a sharp DBTT; they remain ductile to cryogenic temperatures. Consequently, Charpy values for aluminum are generally high and do not discriminate among alloys or tempers as effectively as fracture toughness or tear tests. MMPDS does not list Charpy requirements for most aluminum alloys, and the aerospace community relies instead on K_IC, Kahn tear, and R-curve testing for toughness qualification. **Moderately supported** — based on general metallurgical knowledge; direct citations on Charpy-aluminum limitations were not extracted.

---

## 4. Notched Tension (ASTM E602) and Notch Sensitivity

ASTM E602 covers sharp-notch tension testing to measure the notch tensile strength (NTS) and the notch-strength ratio (NSR = NTS/σ_YS). It reveals notch sensitivity: an alloy with NSR > 1 shows notch strengthening (ductile, redistributes stress), while NSR < 1 indicates notch embrittlement. The test uses circumferentially notched round bars with a 60° notch angle and a specified stress-concentration factor (K_t typically 6–8). For high-strength 7xxx alloys, tear tests with varying notch-root radii distinguished pop-in behavior (sudden failure from sharp notches) from gradual crack propagation, confirming that tensile tests on smooth specimens cannot capture this notch-sensitivity response (pqac-00000006).

---

## 5. Compression Testing (ASTM E9)

ASTM E9 covers uniaxial compression testing using short cylindrical specimens (typically L/D = 1.5–3.0 to avoid buckling). It reveals compressive yield strength (CYS) and work-hardening behavior, which may differ from tension in textured or anisotropic materials. For LPBF metals, compression testing has shown that apparent tensile anisotropy is sometimes due to spatial inhomogeneity rather than intrinsic anisotropy, as confirmed by systematic compressive tests (pqac-00000029). Material consumption is modest (~10 mm diameter × 20 mm cylinders), and tests take minutes.

---

## 6. Shear Testing (ASTM B769, B565, V-Notch)

**ASTM B769** covers double-shear testing of aluminum plate. **ASTM B565** covers pin-type bearing and shear testing for aerospace fastener holes. **V-notch shear** (e.g., Iosipescu) measures in-plane shear strength and modulus. These tests reveal shear strength (typically 55–65% of UTS for aluminum), shear modulus, and the alloy's response to fastener-loading geometries critical in aircraft joints. MMPDS requires shear allowables for structural design. For full A- or B-basis qualification, 20 shear specimens suffice if tensile allowables are already established from 100 specimens (pqac-00000073).

---

## 7. Bearing Testing (ASTM E238)

ASTM E238 measures bearing yield and ultimate strength of sheet and plate by loading a pin through a hole. It reveals the material's resistance to hole elongation under fastener loading. Bearing strength is typically 1.5–2.0× the tensile UTS for aluminum alloys. Test specimens are small plates with a central hole, and multiple specimens can be cut from limited material.

---

## 8. Hardness Testing and Hardness–Yield-Strength Prediction for Aluminum

### Rockwell, Vickers, Brinell

Hardness testing (Rockwell B/F, Vickers HV, Brinell HB) is rapid, semi-destructive, and requires minimal material (a flat surface ≥ several mm²). It is used for quality control, heat-treatment verification, and spatial property mapping.

### Nanoindentation

Nanoindentation probes sub-micron to micron-scale volumes, measuring hardness and elastic modulus via the Oliver-Pharr method. High-throughput nanoindentation can produce 196–225+ indents per specimen in automated mapping modes (pqac-00000037).

### Hardness–Yield-Strength Correlation (Tabor Relation)

The classical Tabor relation links Vickers hardness to flow stress: P_m ≈ C·σ_f, where P_m is the mean contact pressure, C ≈ 2.956 is the constraint factor, and HV = 0.927·P_m. For fully work-hardened material, σ_YS ≈ HV/2.74, giving a slope of ~0.365 (pqac-00000019). For age-hardenable Al-Mg-Si alloys, the relationship is better described with a fitted intercept: σ_YS = 0.383·HV − 101.5, achieving R² = 0.937 (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Most predictions fall within ±15–30% of tensile-measured yield strength, but outliers arise from differing solution treatments, quenching conditions, and highly over-aged states (pqac-00000020). For nanoindentation, the indentation size effect (ISE) causes hardness to increase at depths below ~1–2 μm, complicating direct conversion to bulk yield strength (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Pile-up errors can reach ~60% for pyramidal indenters on non-hardening alloys (pqac-00000021).

**Summary:** Hardness is a useful screening proxy for yield strength within a consistent alloy/temper family but is not universal; material-specific calibration is needed. **Strongly supported.**

---

## 9. Stress-Corrosion Cracking (ASTM G47, G139) and Exfoliation (ASTM G34)

### ASTM G47 — SCC Susceptibility

ASTM G47 determines susceptibility to stress-corrosion cracking in 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloy products by applying sustained tensile stress (typically via C-ring, bolt-loading, or direct tension) in an aggressive environment (usually alternate immersion in 3.5% NaCl solution, 10 min wet / 50 min dry cycles, at ~25 °C) for ≥ 20–30 days (pqac-00000044). It reveals whether an alloy-temper combination will develop SCC under service-relevant conditions.

### ASTM G139 — Breaking Load SCC

ASTM G139 uses a breaking-load method with pre-cracked or smooth specimens exposed to corrosive media under sustained load. It provides a quantitative measure of SCC resistance for heat-treatable aluminum alloy products (pqac-00000044).

**Limitation:** Holroyd et al. (2022) caution that ASTM G47 and G139 may not reliably distinguish the SCC susceptibility of closely performing, relatively resistant alloy tempers and cannot precisely predict service life (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048). **Strongly supported.**

### ASTM G34 — Exfoliation (EXCO Test)

The EXCO test immerses specimens in an aggressive oxidizing acidic chloride solution (4.0 M NaCl + 0.5 M KNO₃ + 0.1 M HNO₃, initial pH ~0.4) for 48–96 hours. Surface appearance is visually rated from N (no attack) through EA–ED (increasing exfoliation severity) (pqac-00000043). This test identifies alloys and tempers susceptible to intergranular corrosion-driven layer-by-layer delamination. It can distinguish resistant and susceptible tempers (e.g., AA7075-T76 vs. T6) but may overstate attack relative to service environments for some alloys (pqac-00000043). **Strongly supported.**

### Residual-Stress Measurement

Residual stresses in LPBF parts are typically measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD), hole-drilling (ASTM E837), neutron diffraction, or contour methods. These are critical because LPBF produces high tensile residual stresses at surfaces that can accelerate fatigue-crack initiation and SCC. Shot peening has been shown to shift surface residual stresses from tension to compression, significantly improving fatigue behavior of LPBF Scalmalloy® (from the Musekamp 2022 study context).

---

## 10. Additive Manufacturing Qualification Standards

### NASA-STD-6030 and MSFC-STD-3716

NASA-STD-6030 is the governing standard for additively manufactured spaceflight hardware. It requires an Additive Manufacturing Control Plan (AMCP), a Material Usage Agreement (MUA) specifying the Material Property Suite (MPS), a Part Production Plan (PPP), and an End Item Data Package (EIDP) (pqac-00000015). Qualification encompasses the complete process from design through flight-ready part, including feedstock control, process parameters, thermal management, post-processing, and in-process monitoring (pqac-00000017). MSFC-STD-3716 was the interim predecessor, developed for the SLS RS-25 program, covering metallic LPBF specifically (pqac-00000016). Both require first-article material-property verification including tensile, fatigue, and fracture testing of witness specimens from every hardware build (pqac-00000015).

### AMS 7032 and AMS 7003

AMS 7032 defines Installation Qualification (IQ), Operational Qualification (OQ), and Performance Qualification (PQ) for AM processes, concepts reflected within the NASA framework though not using identical terminology (pqac-00000017). AMS 7003 covers wire-feed AM processes.

### MMPDS A-Basis and B-Basis Allowables

A-basis (T99): a minimum property value that at least 99% of the population will meet or exceed, with 95% confidence. B-basis (T90): at least 90% will meet or exceed, with 95% confidence (pqac-00000074). Conventional MMPDS requires ≥ 100 specimens from ≥ 10 lots (10 per lot) for full allowable determination; nonparametric distributions may require ≥ 300 observations. A reduced B-basis plan uses ≥ 20 samples from ≥ 3 heats (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000073). For AM, equivalent terminology uses C-basis (= A-basis) and D-basis (= B-basis), reflecting the additional variability from build direction, machine, and location (pqac-00000072). The conventional approach is expensive for AM due to process-dependent variability, motivating model-based and statistically updated approaches using Process Control Reference Distributions (PCRD) (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000077). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 11. Why Fatigue Rather Than Tensile Strength Usually Limits LPBF Aluminum

LPBF aluminum alloys routinely achieve tensile yield strengths comparable to wrought counterparts after heat treatment (e.g., 300–450 MPa for AlSi10Mg). However, fatigue performance is severely degraded by:

- **Surface roughness:** As-built LPBF surfaces have Ra = 1.5–17.6 μm depending on orientation, acting as "killer notches" that nucleate fatigue cracks (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000052). For AlSi10Mg, as-built fatigue strength was only 54 MPa; combined post-processing (blasting + laser treatment + laser cavitation peening) raised it to 103 MPa (from Soyama 2024 context, doi:10.3390/coatings14091174).
- **Porosity:** Subsurface pores (lack-of-fusion and gas porosity) become fatigue-crack initiation sites, especially after machining exposes them. Pore size and location matter more than total porosity (pqac-00000050). HIP reduced porosity by 64% and mean pore diameter by 11% in AlSi10Mg (pqac-00000049).
- **Build orientation:** Lack-of-fusion pores at melt-pool boundaries are especially harmful in vertically built specimens (pqac-00000051). Fatigue limits showed modest orientation dependence (109–118 MPa for Al2024-RAM2 depending on orientation) (pqac-00000052).
- **HIP effects:** HIP closes porosity and can improve fatigue life but may coarsen the Si phase and reduce hardness; post-HIP machining may be needed (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050).

The fundamental reason is that tensile tests average bulk properties over the gauge section, while fatigue failure is controlled by the worst local defect in the stressed volume (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 12. Small-Specimen and Emerging Methods

### Small Punch Test (ASTM E3205)

ASTM E3205-20 specifies an 8 mm diameter × 0.5 mm thick disk specimen clamped between dies and loaded by a 2.5 mm diameter ball (or 1.25 mm radius punch) (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Material volume is only ~25 mm³. The force-displacement curve yields transition force (F_A), maximum force (F_M), failure displacement (U_F), and total energy, from which yield strength and UTS are estimated via empirical correlations (pqac-00000030). SPT has been applied to AM Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, and stainless steels to assess anisotropy, build-orientation effects, heat-treatment response, and spatial property variation within builds (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033). It has also been combined with Jominy bar testing as a high-throughput screening methodology for heat-treatment optimization (from Miguel 2023, doi:10.3390/met13111797). **Strongly supported.**

### Profilometry-Based Indentation Plastometry (PIP)

PIP uses a spherical indenter ball (~0.5–1 mm radius) pressed into the sample to a controlled depth under kN-range loads. After indentation, the three-dimensional residual indent profile is measured by profilometry. Iterative inverse FEM simulation then converges on the best-fit constitutive stress-strain law (typically Voce) by matching predicted and measured profiles (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000064). The characterized volume is a disk of ~1 mm diameter and ~100–200 μm depth, providing ~1–2 mm lateral resolution (pqac-00000064). Commercial automated systems complete indentation, profilometry, and convergence within a few minutes (pqac-00000032). PIP-derived stress-strain curves show excellent agreement with tensile and compressive test data (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000057). For AM metals, PIP has been used to study anisotropy, spatial inhomogeneity, and the effect of build position in LPBF maraging steel, detecting that apparent tensile anisotropy was actually due to build-height inhomogeneity (pqac-00000029). PIP has also been applied to porosity effects in AM stainless steel (from Reiff-Musgrove 2022, doi:10.1002/adem.202200642) and can operate at high temperatures up to 800 °C (from Tammpere 2024, doi:10.1002/adem.202301073). **Strongly supported.**

### Micropillar Compression

FIB-milled micropillars (typically 2 μm diameter, 6–7 μm height) enable single-crystal or single-grain mechanical testing. For AM 316L stainless steel, micropillar compression yielded yield stresses of 431–474 MPa, versus 322 MPa for cast material (from Kurdi 2024, doi:10.3390/ma17020439). This technique reveals crystallographic-orientation-dependent deformation, phase-specific mechanical response, and grain-boundary effects, but exhibits size effects and does not directly measure bulk engineering properties (pqac-00000009). Material consumption is negligible but FIB preparation is slow (~hours per pillar).

### Miniature Tensile Testing and Shear Punch

Miniature tensile specimens (gauge lengths 5–15 mm, cross-sections ~1 × 0.5 mm) can be machined from small volumes of AM material. The shear punch test uses a flat-ended cylindrical punch pushed through a clamped disk, providing shear yield and ultimate strength from even smaller specimens than SPT.

---

## 13. High-Throughput and Automated Mechanical Testing

### Automated Nanoindentation Mapping

High-throughput nanoindentation is the most mature automated screening method. Modern systems achieve hundreds to thousands of indents per sample using Accelerated Property Mapping (XPM), with individual indent contact times as short as 0.2 s (versus 20 s conventional), reducing drift by two orders of magnitude (pqac-00000037). Hoefler et al. (2025) demonstrated 2,400 nanoindentation + SEM data points in 13 days on a single gradient-aged superalloy sample—approximately 200× faster than conventional tensile testing for equivalent data volume. Each indent required an average of 188 s including loading, while automated SEM imaging took ~44 s per position (pqac-00000038). The total preparation + measurement time was 314 hours (pqac-00000038).

### HT-READ (High-Throughput Rapid Experimental Alloy Development)

Vecchio et al. (2021) developed HT-READ, an integrated closed-loop framework combining CALPHAD computation, directed-energy-deposition fabrication of 16-composition libraries via an Alloy Development Feeder, and automated characterization including XRD (~10 min/sample), SEM-EDS/EBSD (~1 min/sample), and nanoindentation (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). Machine-learning (Automatminer) correctly identified three of the five hardest compositions from the 16-member library (pqac-00000066). **Strongly supported.**

### Combinatorial Approaches

Diffusion multiples create continuous composition gradients across ternary systems; scanning nanoindentation then maps hardness and modulus across the gradient at ~1,000× the efficiency of one-at-a-time testing (pqac-00000034). Microfabricated cantilever beam arrays enable parallel thin-film property measurement, and MEMS-based tensile arrays allow parallel microtensile testing (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000041). SPT on Jominy bars has been demonstrated for high-throughput screening of heat-treatment effects (from Miguel 2023, doi:10.3390/met13111797).

### Robotic Test Cells

Fully robotic mechanical-testing cells integrating specimen handling, testing, and data analysis are an emerging capability referenced in the literature but not yet widely documented for aluminum alloy screening in peer-reviewed studies. **Weakly supported.**

---

## 14. Summary Recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

Given that the BYU lab designs LPBF aluminum alloys with AI and CALPHAD, makes powder by ultrasonic atomization, and currently tests through single tracks, density cubes, and room-temperature tensile bars, the following tests should be prioritized for addition:

**Highest priority (fatigue-critical for LPBF aluminum):**
1. **High-cycle fatigue (ASTM E466):** Because fatigue, not tensile strength, is the life-limiting property for LPBF aluminum. Surface roughness, porosity, and build orientation all govern fatigue performance.
2. **Automated nanoindentation mapping:** For rapid screening of hardness-composition-microstructure relationships across alloy libraries—the most automatable and highest-throughput mechanical test available (~200× faster than tensile).
3. **Small punch testing (ASTM E3205):** For estimating tensile properties from minimal material (25 mm³ per specimen), enabling screening of many compositions.

**High priority (qualification-essential):**
4. **Fracture toughness (ASTM E399/E1820) or Kahn tear test (B871):** Kahn tear testing is recommended first due to low material requirements and suitability for sheet/thin specimens.
5. **Fatigue crack growth (ASTM E647):** Required for damage-tolerance certification.
6. **Stress-corrosion cracking (ASTM G47) and exfoliation (G34):** Essential for any alloy intended for service in humid or marine environments.

**Medium priority (supplementary/screening):**
7. **PIP (profilometry-based indentation plastometry):** Full stress-strain curves from minimal material in minutes, with demonstrated applicability to AM metals.
8. **Elevated-temperature tensile testing:** For alloys targeting thermal stability.
9. **Compression testing (ASTM E9):** To verify isotropy and characterize compressive properties.

**Lower priority (specialized):**
10. **Charpy impact (E23):** Low discriminating power for aluminum alloys.
11. **Bearing (E238) and shear (B769, B565):** Needed only for specific joint-design qualification.
12. **Micropillar compression:** Valuable for understanding single-grain behavior but not for engineering qualification.

---

## Strength of Evidence Assessment

| Claim | Support Level |
|-------|---------------|
| Fracture toughness tests reveal damage tolerance that tensile cannot | **Strong** |
| Kahn tear test specimen sizes and unit energies | **Strong** |
| Fatigue limits LPBF aluminum due to surface/porosity defects | **Strong** |
| ASTM G34 EXCO solution and exposure conditions | **Strong** |
| Hardness predicts Al yield strength within ±15–30% with calibration | **Strong** |
| MMPDS A/B-basis definitions and specimen requirements | **Strong** |
| NASA-STD-6030 qualification framework | **Strong** |
| Automated nanoindentation achieves ~200× faster screening | **Strong** |
| PIP provides accurate stress-strain curves for AM metals | **Strong** |
| SPT ASTM E3205 specimen dimensions and AM applicability | **Strong** |
| HT-READ methodology for combinatorial alloy screening | **Strong** |
| Charpy is little used for aluminum due to no DBTT | **Moderate** |
| Robotic test cells for alloy screening | **Weak** |
| Ultrasonic fatigue specific LPBF aluminum data | **Moderate** |
| AMS 7032/7003 detailed requirements | **Moderate** |
"}
