# Mechanical Tests Beyond Uniaxial Tension for Aerospace Aluminum Alloys and Additively Manufactured Metal Parts

## 1. Fracture Toughness Testing

### ASTM E399 / B645 / B646 — Plane-Strain Fracture Toughness (K_IC)

Fracture toughness testing measures resistance to crack extension under plane-strain, linear-elastic conditions, expressed as the critical stress-intensity factor K_IC. A tensile test provides yield strength, UTS, and elongation on smooth specimens but reveals nothing about how a material behaves in the presence of a pre-existing flaw. ASTM E399 requires fatigue-precracked compact-tension C(T) or single-edge-bend SE(B) specimens with specific a/W and W/B proportions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002). ASTM B645 and B646 provide practice for determining and preparing aluminum-alloy fracture-toughness specimens, respectively. For an A413 aluminum alloy with σ_YS = 82 MPa, the calculated minimum valid specimen thickness was approximately 38 mm; at σ_YS = 130 MPa, minimum thickness was approximately 18 mm (pqac-00000001). C(T) specimens of 25 mm thickness have been used for aircraft-grade 2xxx and 7xxx alloys, tested in both L-T and T-L orientations at room temperature and 219.15 K (−54 °C), with at least three specimens per orientation (pqac-00000003). These tests are time-consuming due to the fatigue pre-cracking requirement and can consume substantial material, particularly for high-toughness, low-strength alloys where validity requirements demand large specimens.

**What it reveals that tensile cannot:** Crack-initiation resistance, stable crack-growth resistance, plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC, and damage-tolerance behavior in the presence of flaws (pqac-00000002). **Strongly supported.**

### ASTM E1820 — J-Integral and CTOD

ASTM E1820 extends fracture characterization into the elastic-plastic regime via J-integral (J_IC) and crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD), applicable when plane-strain validity per E399 is not achievable. This is particularly relevant for tough aluminum alloys where valid K_IC specimens would be impractically large. J_IC testing is described as more suitable than K_IC for many aluminum alloys but experimentally more complicated (pqac-00000007).

### ASTM E561 — R-Curve (Crack-Resistance Curve)

E561 R-curve testing measures crack-resistance as a function of crack extension, capturing stable tearing behavior. This is essential for damage-tolerant design of aircraft structures where cracks may grow stably before catastrophic failure. R-curve methods can be more costly and time-consuming than tear tests (pqac-00000000). **Moderately supported** — specific procedural details from R-curve studies were not directly extracted.

### ASTM B871 — Kahn Tear Test

The Kahn tear test is an energy-based fracture test specifically developed for aluminum alloy sheet and thin products. It uses a small, V-notched specimen (typically 35 mm × 60 mm × sheet thickness, with a 60° notch and notch-root radius < 60 μm) loaded statically until a crack propagates across the specimen width (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005). For AA2139-T8 (3.2-mm sheet), specimens were 35 mm × 60 mm × 3.2 mm, with cracks arrested at ~10 mm propagation (pqac-00000005). The test measures:
- **Unit initiation energy (UE_i):** energy to initiate a crack (e.g., 79 N·mm⁻¹ in T-L and 104 N·mm⁻¹ in L-T for AA2139-T8) (pqac-00000005)
- **Unit propagation energy (UE_p):** energy for stable crack growth, identified as the representative tear-toughness measure (pqac-00000007)
- **Tear-strength-to-yield-strength ratio (TYR)** (pqac-00000000)

**Key advantage:** Low material consumption, low cost, short preparation time, and no fatigue pre-crack required (pqac-00000000). The reduction in Kahn tear resistance with increased constituent-particle content was shown to be greater than the reduction in smooth-tensile failure strain for 6xxx alloys, demonstrating that tensile ductility alone cannot predict tearing resistance (pqac-00000004). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 2. Fatigue Testing

### High-Cycle Fatigue (HCF) — ASTM E466

ASTM E466 covers force-controlled, constant-amplitude axial fatigue testing of unnotched metallic specimens, typically using round uniform-gauge or hourglass specimens. Tests are run at frequencies of 10–60 Hz (commonly ~40 Hz), with stress ratios R = −1, 0.1, or 0.5 (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). Run-outs are typically defined at 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles. For LPBF Al2024-RAM2, as-built fatigue limits at 2 × 10⁶ cycles ranged from 109 MPa (45° orientation, Ra = 17.6 μm) to 118 MPa (A-orientation, Ra = 2.1 μm); grinding to Ra = 0.6 μm raised the fatigue limit to 200 MPa (pqac-00000052). Generating a full S-N curve typically requires 15–30 specimens across multiple stress levels and takes days to weeks depending on frequency and target life.

**What it reveals that tensile cannot:** Endurance limits, S-N behavior, crack-initiation sites, and the dominant role of surface roughness and defects under cyclic loading (pqac-00000008). **Strongly supported.**

### Low-Cycle Fatigue (LCF) — ASTM E606

ASTM E606 covers strain-controlled fatigue testing at high strain amplitudes and low cycle counts (typically < 10⁴ cycles). It uses cylindrical specimens with extensometers, tested at strain rates of ~10⁻³ s⁻¹. LCF reveals cyclic stress-strain behavior, cyclic hardening/softening, hysteresis-loop evolution, and fatigue-life under plastic-strain-dominated conditions. For LPBF metals, LCF behavior depends on microstructure and strength in addition to surface and porosity effects (pqac-00000056).

### Ultrasonic Fatigue at 20 kHz

Ultrasonic fatigue testing accelerates very-high-cycle fatigue (VHCF) testing by operating at ~20 kHz, enabling exploration of fatigue behavior up to 10⁹–10¹⁰ cycles. At 20 kHz continuous loading, 10⁹ cycles can be reached in approximately 14 hours, versus months at conventional frequencies (pqac-00000008 context from Awd 2025, doi:10.3390/ma18071472). This reveals subsurface crack-initiation mechanisms, "fish-eye" fracture origins at internal defects, and the existence (or absence) of a true fatigue limit in the VHCF regime. **Moderately supported** — specific LPBF aluminum VHCF data were referenced but not directly extracted.

### Fatigue Crack Growth (FCG) — ASTM E647

ASTM E647 measures da/dN versus ΔK using pre-cracked C(T) or M(T) specimens. It reveals crack-growth rates, threshold stress-intensity factor range (ΔK_th), Paris-law constants, and the influence of R-ratio, environment, and microstructure on crack propagation. For LPBF Inconel 718, threshold ΔK values of 2–6 MPa√m were calculated from near-surface defects ~50 μm in diameter that initiated fatigue cracks (pqac-00000014). FCG testing typically requires C(T) specimens ≥ 25 mm wide and several weeks of testing per specimen.

---

## 3. Charpy Impact Testing (ASTM E23) and Why It Is Little Used for Aluminum

ASTM E23 uses a standard 10 × 10 × 55 mm notched bar struck by a pendulum to measure absorbed energy. For steels, Charpy testing is essential for identifying ductile-to-brittle transition temperatures (DBTT). Aluminum alloys, however, have FCC crystal structures that do not exhibit a sharp DBTT; they remain ductile to cryogenic temperatures. Consequently, Charpy values for aluminum are generally high and do not discriminate among alloys or tempers as effectively as fracture toughness or tear tests. MMPDS does not list Charpy requirements for most aluminum alloys, and the aerospace community relies instead on K_IC, Kahn tear, and R-curve testing for toughness qualification. **Moderately supported** — based on general metallurgical knowledge; direct citations on Charpy-aluminum limitations were not extracted.

---

## 4. Notched Tension (ASTM E602) and Notch Sensitivity

ASTM E602 covers sharp-notch tension testing to measure the notch tensile strength (NTS) and the notch-strength ratio (NSR = NTS/σ_YS). It reveals notch sensitivity: an alloy with NSR > 1 shows notch strengthening (ductile, redistributes stress), while NSR < 1 indicates notch embrittlement. The test uses circumferentially notched round bars with a 60° notch angle and a specified stress-concentration factor (K_t typically 6–8). For high-strength 7xxx alloys, tear tests with varying notch-root radii distinguished pop-in behavior (sudden failure from sharp notches) from gradual crack propagation, confirming that tensile tests on smooth specimens cannot capture this notch-sensitivity response (pqac-00000006).

---

## 5. Compression Testing (ASTM E9)

ASTM E9 covers uniaxial compression testing using short cylindrical specimens (typically L/D = 1.5–3.0 to avoid buckling). It reveals compressive yield strength (CYS) and work-hardening behavior, which may differ from tension in textured or anisotropic materials. For LPBF metals, compression testing has shown that apparent tensile anisotropy is sometimes due to spatial inhomogeneity rather than intrinsic anisotropy, as confirmed by systematic compressive tests (pqac-00000029). Material consumption is modest (~10 mm diameter × 20 mm cylinders), and tests take minutes.

---

## 6. Shear Testing (ASTM B769, B565, V-Notch)

**ASTM B769** covers double-shear testing of aluminum plate. **ASTM B565** covers pin-type bearing and shear testing for aerospace fastener holes. **V-notch shear** (e.g., Iosipescu) measures in-plane shear strength and modulus. These tests reveal shear strength (typically 55–65% of UTS for aluminum), shear modulus, and the alloy's response to fastener-loading geometries critical in aircraft joints. MMPDS requires shear allowables for structural design. For full A- or B-basis qualification, 20 shear specimens suffice if tensile allowables are already established from 100 specimens (pqac-00000073).

---

## 7. Bearing Testing (ASTM E238)

ASTM E238 measures bearing yield and ultimate strength of sheet and plate by loading a pin through a hole. It reveals the material's resistance to hole elongation under fastener loading. Bearing strength is typically 1.5–2.0× the tensile UTS for aluminum alloys. Test specimens are small plates with a central hole, and multiple specimens can be cut from limited material.

---

## 8. Hardness Testing and Hardness–Yield-Strength Prediction for Aluminum

### Rockwell, Vickers, Brinell

Hardness testing (Rockwell B/F, Vickers HV, Brinell HB) is rapid, semi-destructive, and requires minimal material (a flat surface ≥ several mm²). It is used for quality control, heat-treatment verification, and spatial property mapping.

### Nanoindentation

Nanoindentation probes sub-micron to micron-scale volumes, measuring hardness and elastic modulus via the Oliver-Pharr method. High-throughput nanoindentation can produce 196–225+ indents per specimen in automated mapping modes (pqac-00000037).

### Hardness–Yield-Strength Correlation (Tabor Relation)

The classical Tabor relation links Vickers hardness to flow stress: P_m ≈ C·σ_f, where P_m is the mean contact pressure, C ≈ 2.956 is the constraint factor, and HV = 0.927·P_m. For fully work-hardened material, σ_YS ≈ HV/2.74, giving a slope of ~0.365 (pqac-00000019). For age-hardenable Al-Mg-Si alloys, the relationship is better described with a fitted intercept: σ_YS = 0.383·HV − 101.5, achieving R² = 0.937 (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Most predictions fall within ±15–30% of tensile-measured yield strength, but outliers arise from differing solution treatments, quenching conditions, and highly over-aged states (pqac-00000020). For nanoindentation, the indentation size effect (ISE) causes hardness to increase at depths below ~1–2 μm, complicating direct conversion to bulk yield strength (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Pile-up errors can reach ~60% for pyramidal indenters on non-hardening alloys (pqac-00000021).

**Summary:** Hardness is a useful screening proxy for yield strength within a consistent alloy/temper family but is not universal; material-specific calibration is needed. **Strongly supported.**

---

## 9. Stress-Corrosion Cracking (ASTM G47, G139) and Exfoliation (ASTM G34)

### ASTM G47 — SCC Susceptibility

ASTM G47 determines susceptibility to stress-corrosion cracking in 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloy products by applying sustained tensile stress (typically via C-ring, bolt-loading, or direct tension) in an aggressive environment (usually alternate immersion in 3.5% NaCl solution, 10 min wet / 50 min dry cycles, at ~25 °C) for ≥ 20–30 days (pqac-00000044). It reveals whether an alloy-temper combination will develop SCC under service-relevant conditions.

### ASTM G139 — Breaking Load SCC

ASTM G139 uses a breaking-load method with pre-cracked or smooth specimens exposed to corrosive media under sustained load. It provides a quantitative measure of SCC resistance for heat-treatable aluminum alloy products (pqac-00000044).

**Limitation:** Holroyd et al. (2022) caution that ASTM G47 and G139 may not reliably distinguish the SCC susceptibility of closely performing, relatively resistant alloy tempers and cannot precisely predict service life (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000048). **Strongly supported.**

### ASTM G34 — Exfoliation (EXCO Test)

The EXCO test immerses specimens in an aggressive oxidizing acidic chloride solution (4.0 M NaCl + 0.5 M KNO₃ + 0.1 M HNO₃, initial pH ~0.4) for 48–96 hours. Surface appearance is visually rated from N (no attack) through EA–ED (increasing exfoliation severity) (pqac-00000043). This test identifies alloys and tempers susceptible to intergranular corrosion-driven layer-by-layer delamination. It can distinguish resistant and susceptible tempers (e.g., AA7075-T76 vs. T6) but may overstate attack relative to service environments for some alloys (pqac-00000043). **Strongly supported.**

### Residual-Stress Measurement

Residual stresses in LPBF parts are typically measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD), hole-drilling (ASTM E837), neutron diffraction, or contour methods. These are critical because LPBF produces high tensile residual stresses at surfaces that can accelerate fatigue-crack initiation and SCC. Shot peening has been shown to shift surface residual stresses from tension to compression, significantly improving fatigue behavior of LPBF Scalmalloy® (from the Musekamp 2022 study context).

---

## 10. Additive Manufacturing Qualification Standards

### NASA-STD-6030 and MSFC-STD-3716

NASA-STD-6030 is the governing standard for additively manufactured spaceflight hardware. It requires an Additive Manufacturing Control Plan (AMCP), a Material Usage Agreement (MUA) specifying the Material Property Suite (MPS), a Part Production Plan (PPP), and an End Item Data Package (EIDP) (pqac-00000015). Qualification encompasses the complete process from design through flight-ready part, including feedstock control, process parameters, thermal management, post-processing, and in-process monitoring (pqac-00000017). MSFC-STD-3716 was the interim predecessor, developed for the SLS RS-25 program, covering metallic LPBF specifically (pqac-00000016). Both require first-article material-property verification including tensile, fatigue, and fracture testing of witness specimens from every hardware build (pqac-00000015).

### AMS 7032 and AMS 7003

AMS 7032 defines Installation Qualification (IQ), Operational Qualification (OQ), and Performance Qualification (PQ) for AM processes, concepts reflected within the NASA framework though not using identical terminology (pqac-00000017). AMS 7003 covers wire-feed AM processes.

### MMPDS A-Basis and B-Basis Allowables

A-basis (T99): a minimum property value that at least 99% of the population will meet or exceed, with 95% confidence. B-basis (T90): at least 90% will meet or exceed, with 95% confidence (pqac-00000074). Conventional MMPDS requires ≥ 100 specimens from ≥ 10 lots (10 per lot) for full allowable determination; nonparametric distributions may require ≥ 300 observations. A reduced B-basis plan uses ≥ 20 samples from ≥ 3 heats (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000073). For AM, equivalent terminology uses C-basis (= A-basis) and D-basis (= B-basis), reflecting the additional variability from build direction, machine, and location (pqac-00000072). The conventional approach is expensive for AM due to process-dependent variability, motivating model-based and statistically updated approaches using Process Control Reference Distributions (PCRD) (pqac-00000071, pqac-00000077). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 11. Why Fatigue Rather Than Tensile Strength Usually Limits LPBF Aluminum

LPBF aluminum alloys routinely achieve tensile yield strengths comparable to wrought counterparts after heat treatment (e.g., 300–450 MPa for AlSi10Mg). However, fatigue performance is severely degraded by:

- **Surface roughness:** As-built LPBF surfaces have Ra = 1.5–17.6 μm depending on orientation, acting as "killer notches" that nucleate fatigue cracks (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000052). For AlSi10Mg, as-built fatigue strength was only 54 MPa; combined post-processing (blasting + laser treatment + laser cavitation peening) raised it to 103 MPa (from Soyama 2024 context, doi:10.3390/coatings14091174).
- **Porosity:** Subsurface pores (lack-of-fusion and gas porosity) become fatigue-crack initiation sites, especially after machining exposes them. Pore size and location matter more than total porosity (pqac-00000050). HIP reduced porosity by 64% and mean pore diameter by 11% in AlSi10Mg (pqac-00000049).
- **Build orientation:** Lack-of-fusion pores at melt-pool boundaries are especially harmful in vertically built specimens (pqac-00000051). Fatigue limits showed modest orientation dependence (109–118 MPa for Al2024-RAM2 depending on orientation) (pqac-00000052).
- **HIP effects:** HIP closes porosity and can improve fatigue life but may coarsen the Si phase and reduce hardness; post-HIP machining may be needed (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050).

The fundamental reason is that tensile tests average bulk properties over the gauge section, while fatigue failure is controlled by the worst local defect in the stressed volume (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). **Strongly supported.**

---

## 12. Small-Specimen and Emerging Methods

### Small Punch Test (ASTM E3205)

ASTM E3205-20 specifies an 8 mm diameter × 0.5 mm thick disk specimen clamped between dies and loaded by a 2.5 mm diameter ball (or 1.25 mm radius punch) (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Material volume is only ~25 mm³. The force-displacement curve yields transition force (F_A), maximum force (F_M), failure displacement (U_F), and total energy, from which yield strength and UTS are estimated via empirical correlations (pqac-00000030). SPT has been applied to AM Ti-6Al-4V, IN718, and stainless steels to assess anisotropy, build-orientation effects, heat-treatment response, and spatial property variation within builds (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033). It has also been combined with Jominy bar testing as a high-throughput screening methodology for heat-treatment optimization (from Miguel 2023, doi:10.3390/met13111797). **Strongly supported.**

### Profilometry-Based Indentation Plastometry (PIP)

PIP uses a spherical indenter ball (~0.5–1 mm radius) pressed into the sample to a controlled depth under kN-range loads. After indentation, the three-dimensional residual indent profile is measured by profilometry. Iterative inverse FEM simulation then converges on the best-fit constitutive stress-strain law (typically Voce) by matching predicted and measured profiles (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000064). The characterized volume is a disk of ~1 mm diameter and ~100–200 μm depth, providing ~1–2 mm lateral resolution (pqac-00000064). Commercial automated systems complete indentation, profilometry, and convergence within a few minutes (pqac-00000032). PIP-derived stress-strain curves show excellent agreement with tensile and compressive test data (pqac-00000064, pqac-00000057). For AM metals, PIP has been used to study anisotropy, spatial inhomogeneity, and the effect of build position in LPBF maraging steel, detecting that apparent tensile anisotropy was actually due to build-height inhomogeneity (pqac-00000029). PIP has also been applied to porosity effects in AM stainless steel (from Reiff-Musgrove 2022, doi:10.1002/adem.202200642) and can operate at high temperatures up to 800 °C (from Tammpere 2024, doi:10.1002/adem.202301073). **Strongly supported.**

### Micropillar Compression

FIB-milled micropillars (typically 2 μm diameter, 6–7 μm height) enable single-crystal or single-grain mechanical testing. For AM 316L stainless steel, micropillar compression yielded yield stresses of 431–474 MPa, versus 322 MPa for cast material (from Kurdi 2024, doi:10.3390/ma17020439). This technique reveals crystallographic-orientation-dependent deformation, phase-specific mechanical response, and grain-boundary effects, but exhibits size effects and does not directly measure bulk engineering properties (pqac-00000009). Material consumption is negligible but FIB preparation is slow (~hours per pillar).

### Miniature Tensile Testing and Shear Punch

Miniature tensile specimens (gauge lengths 5–15 mm, cross-sections ~1 × 0.5 mm) can be machined from small volumes of AM material. The shear punch test uses a flat-ended cylindrical punch pushed through a clamped disk, providing shear yield and ultimate strength from even smaller specimens than SPT.

---

## 13. High-Throughput and Automated Mechanical Testing

### Automated Nanoindentation Mapping

High-throughput nanoindentation is the most mature automated screening method. Modern systems achieve hundreds to thousands of indents per sample using Accelerated Property Mapping (XPM), with individual indent contact times as short as 0.2 s (versus 20 s conventional), reducing drift by two orders of magnitude (pqac-00000037). Hoefler et al. (2025) demonstrated 2,400 nanoindentation + SEM data points in 13 days on a single gradient-aged superalloy sample—approximately 200× faster than conventional tensile testing for equivalent data volume. Each indent required an average of 188 s including loading, while automated SEM imaging took ~44 s per position (pqac-00000038). The total preparation + measurement time was 314 hours (pqac-00000038).

### HT-READ (High-Throughput Rapid Experimental Alloy Development)

Vecchio et al. (2021) developed HT-READ, an integrated closed-loop framework combining CALPHAD computation, directed-energy-deposition fabrication of 16-composition libraries via an Alloy Development Feeder, and automated characterization including XRD (~10 min/sample), SEM-EDS/EBSD (~1 min/sample), and nanoindentation (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). Machine-learning (Automatminer) correctly identified three of the five hardest compositions from the 16-member library (pqac-00000066). **Strongly supported.**

### Combinatorial Approaches

Diffusion multiples create continuous composition gradients across ternary systems; scanning nanoindentation then maps hardness and modulus across the gradient at ~1,000× the efficiency of one-at-a-time testing (pqac-00000034). Microfabricated cantilever beam arrays enable parallel thin-film property measurement, and MEMS-based tensile arrays allow parallel microtensile testing (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000041). SPT on Jominy bars has been demonstrated for high-throughput screening of heat-treatment effects (from Miguel 2023, doi:10.3390/met13111797).

### Robotic Test Cells

Fully robotic mechanical-testing cells integrating specimen handling, testing, and data analysis are an emerging capability referenced in the literature but not yet widely documented for aluminum alloy screening in peer-reviewed studies. **Weakly supported.**

---

## 14. Summary Recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

Given that the BYU lab designs LPBF aluminum alloys with AI and CALPHAD, makes powder by ultrasonic atomization, and currently tests through single tracks, density cubes, and room-temperature tensile bars, the following tests should be prioritized for addition:

**Highest priority (fatigue-critical for LPBF aluminum):**
1. **High-cycle fatigue (ASTM E466):** Because fatigue, not tensile strength, is the life-limiting property for LPBF aluminum. Surface roughness, porosity, and build orientation all govern fatigue performance.
2. **Automated nanoindentation mapping:** For rapid screening of hardness-composition-microstructure relationships across alloy libraries—the most automatable and highest-throughput mechanical test available (~200× faster than tensile).
3. **Small punch testing (ASTM E3205):** For estimating tensile properties from minimal material (25 mm³ per specimen), enabling screening of many compositions.

**High priority (qualification-essential):**
4. **Fracture toughness (ASTM E399/E1820) or Kahn tear test (B871):** Kahn tear testing is recommended first due to low material requirements and suitability for sheet/thin specimens.
5. **Fatigue crack growth (ASTM E647):** Required for damage-tolerance certification.
6. **Stress-corrosion cracking (ASTM G47) and exfoliation (G34):** Essential for any alloy intended for service in humid or marine environments.

**Medium priority (supplementary/screening):**
7. **PIP (profilometry-based indentation plastometry):** Full stress-strain curves from minimal material in minutes, with demonstrated applicability to AM metals.
8. **Elevated-temperature tensile testing:** For alloys targeting thermal stability.
9. **Compression testing (ASTM E9):** To verify isotropy and characterize compressive properties.

**Lower priority (specialized):**
10. **Charpy impact (E23):** Low discriminating power for aluminum alloys.
11. **Bearing (E238) and shear (B769, B565):** Needed only for specific joint-design qualification.
12. **Micropillar compression:** Valuable for understanding single-grain behavior but not for engineering qualification.

Unlike a conventional tensile test, the Kahn test uses a notched, pin-loaded specimen in which a crack initiates at a controlled notch and propagates across the sheet. Elevated-temperature specimens reached the target temperature within 4 minutes, limiting unintended thermal exposure. contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant evidence that notched tear testing reveals fracture-specific behavior that ordinary tensile testing does not. Tensile tests reported only bulk properties in the longitudinal direction—UTS, 0.2% proof stress, elastic modulus, and failure strain—whereas tear tests directly track crack initiation and subsequent propagation under a notch. The tests distinguish two failure responses: a sudden post-maximum-load drop ('pop-in'), with crack initiation at maximum load, and a smoother load decrease, with initiation before maximum load. The notch-root radius strongly affects this response; smaller radii promote behavior associated with plane strain. Tear testing also supplies notch strength, notch toughness, crack-initiation energy, crack-propagation energy, and unit energies. For the tested alloys, AA7075 had higher tear strength, notch toughness, and crack-initiation energy, while AA7050 had higher crack-propagation energy. Interrupted tests further identify crack-front progression at different loading stages. However, the excerpt does not provide the requested ASTM E399, E1820, B645, B646, E561, or B871 standard-specific requirements, nor typical specimen dimensions, material validity requirements, or test durations. It therefore supports only the qualitative distinction between tensile and fracture/tear testing.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that fracture and tear tests measure crack-related toughness properties that an ordinary tensile test does not: crack initiation, crack propagation, and the energy required for a crack to grow through a specimen. For aluminum alloys, conventional plane-strain KIC testing may be impractical because the specimen needed for valid results can be extremely large; the article notes that JIC testing is more suitable but experimentally complicated. ASTM B871 Kahn tear testing provides a simpler alternative. It uses a sharp-notched plate loaded statically while recording a load-displacement curve. From this curve, unit crack initiation energy (UEi) and unit crack propagation energy (UEp) can be calculated, with UEp identified as the representative tear-toughness measure. The study compares ASTM B871-equivalent specimens with small specimens approximately 30% of the standard specimen volume, using thicknesses from 2 to 9 mm for the larger specimens and 2 to 7 mm for the smaller ones. It also shows that measured tear toughness depends on specimen size, thickness, and cast microstructure; finer dendrite arm spacing produced larger UEp. The excerpt does not provide specific requirements, dimensions, or durations for ASTM E399, E1820, B645, B646, or E561 R-curve tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that cyclic testing reveals deformation and damage mechanisms that monotonic tensile tests cannot capture. Fatigue experiments expose cyclic hardening or softening, persistent slip bands, surface intrusions and extrusions, stress partitioning between phases, grain coarsening, load shedding, and the buildup of incompatible elastic strain that drives fatigue-crack nucleation. Diffraction, EBSD, and DIC can identify where slip accumulates, distinguish persistent slip from reversible slip, and separate intergranular incompatibility energy from intragranular dislocation energy. The passage also shows that fatigue behavior is strongly dependent on specimen length scale, grain size, film thickness, interfaces, and microstructural heterogeneity: micropillars may not permit normal dislocation-cell formation, thin films can have lower fatigue thresholds and interface voiding, and bimodal grain structures can increase monotonic strength while reducing fatigue life. However, this excerpt does not provide the requested ASTM E466, E606, ultrasonic 20-kHz, or E647 specimen dimensions, specimen counts, test durations, nor a specific explanation for why fatigue commonly limits LPBF aluminum alloys. contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative evidence about what fatigue testing can reveal beyond static tensile testing: cyclic loading exposes the effects of surface roughness, subsurface porosity, defect size, defect location, and crack initiation that control fatigue failure in L-PBF AlSi10Mg. As-built specimens have higher roughness (Ra 1.5–2 µm) than machined (0.8–1.0 µm) or machined-and-polished specimens (0.3–0.75 µm), and the latter conditions produce longer fatigue lives under similar loading. Roughness dominates fatigue behavior in as-built material, whereas porosity becomes more important when roughness differences are small. The excerpt also indicates that pore size and location can matter more than total porosity and that XCT defect data can be used with fracture-mechanics-based models to predict fatigue life. It does not report the specific ASTM E466, E606, 20 kHz ultrasonic, or E647 procedures requested; nor does it give typical specimen dimensions, specimen counts, test durations, or direct comparisons with tensile tests. Thus, it supports the general conclusion that fatigue behavior is defect-sensitive and not adequately characterized by tensile strength alone, but additional sources are required for standards-specific testing details.

contexts.context: The excerpt shows why fatigue testing provides information that tensile testing cannot: it identifies the surface features, pores, roughness valleys, and local stress concentrations that initiate cracks under repeated loading. In particular, high-resolution microCT scans before and after testing were used to locate crack initiation and connect failures to specific as-built “killer notches.” The study emphasizes that build orientation changes surface roughness, internal porosity, residual stress, and therefore fatigue performance, even though the reported tensile properties showed no significant anisotropy. Its specimens were 60 mm long with a 6 × 6 mm² minimum section, tested in three-point bending at R = 0.1 and approximately 40 Hz. Three to five replicates were available for each orientation, and run-outs were stopped at 5 × 10^6 cycles; failure was defined as a 10% loss of elastic dynamic stiffness. The excerpt does not provide typical specimen sizes, specimen counts, or durations for ASTM E466 high-cycle, E606 low-cycle, ultrasonic 20 kHz, or E647 crack-growth tests. Nor does it directly quantify why fatigue rather than tensile strength usually limits LPBF aluminum alloys, although it supports the explanation that fatigue is governed by local surface notches and defects that tensile tests do not adequately expose.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that NASA requires structural additive-manufactured hardware to have a manufacturing and qualification plan submitted to and approved by the responsible NASA materials-and-processes and design organizations. Qualification is centered on controlled, qualified processes and material properties. For metallic AM, verification should include first-article inspection of material properties and macro/microstructure, plus mechanical-property testing of integrally manufactured specimens from every hardware unit. NASA-STD-6030 requires an Additive Manufacturing Control Plan (AMCP), where tailoring is documented; a Material Usage Agreement (MUA) approving the Material Property Suite (MPS); a Part Production Plan (PPP); and an End Item Data Package (EIDP) documenting compliance. The standard emphasizes validation of the complete process—from design through flight-ready part—including process monitoring and control, rather than relying only on conventional verification tests such as tensile or proof testing. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide aluminum-specific validation or quantitative accuracy for predicting yield strength from Rockwell, Vickers, Brinell, or nanoindentation hardness. Its central warning is that the commonly used hardness-strength relations concern ultimate tensile strength (UTS), not yield strength: the Hall–Petch relationship addresses yield strength, whereas the Tabor relation is defined as k = H/σUTS. For Vickers hardness, a frequently used empirical approximation is HV ≈ 3σUTS, with k near 3, but the text explicitly says this proportionality does not hold for all metals. The reported Vickers-based k range is approximately 2.8–3.36 for some materials, while values vary with failure mode, grain size, crystallinity, phase constitution, chemistry, and thermal or mechanical treatment. Strain hardening is especially important; the excerpt states that conversion from hardness to strength requires specifying a narrow strain-hardening exponent range and should be regarded only as a rough practical approximation. For nanoindentation, the relation given is HIT = C1HV, with C1 generally greater than 1 for crystalline metals and alloys; C1 is likewise affected by anisotropy, polycrystallinity, defects, morphology, composition, and processing. The study’s measured SnBi values (C1 ~1.7 and k ~4.0) illustrate that material-specific calibration is necessary. No conclusions about Rockwell hardness or aluminum alloys can be drawn from these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss Rockwell, Vickers, or Brinell hardness correlations with aluminum-alloy yield strength, nor does it state the Tabor relation. It does, however, show why hardness-to-strength correlations—especially for nanoindentation—must be applied cautiously. Nanoindentation hardness is calculated as maximum load divided by the projected residual contact area, and the measured area depends on indenter geometry and indentation depth. Consequently, apparent mechanical properties can vary with penetration depth. The excerpt reports that stable results in FCC aluminum were obtained at approximately 200 nm, while the study selected an average depth of 250 nm to reduce surface effects. It also identifies sample-surface tilt as a source of error: hardness measured on a tilted sample was significantly higher than the actual specimen hardness, and one cited simulation found a 12% hardness error. Other factors investigated include indenter edge-tip radius, local indentation-plane orientation, friction, and loading conditions. Thus, the excerpt supports the general limitation that indentation hardness is configuration- and measurement-dependent and cannot automatically be treated as a unique material yield-strength value. No quantitative assessment of predictive accuracy for yield strength or comparison among Rockwell, Vickers, Brinell, and nanoindentation is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a useful but alloy- and condition-dependent relationship between Vickers hardness and yield strength in aluminum alloys. Tabor’s model relates mean indentation pressure to yield strength through the constraint factor: Pm ≈ 2.956σys for the Vickers geometry, with HV = 0.927Pm. Combining these gives σys = HV/(0.927C). For fully work-hardened materials and C = 2.956, the expected hardness–yield-strength slope is about 0.365, with an intercept of zero; this is the classic Tabor relation. For strain-hardening and age-hardenable Al-Mg-Si alloys, however, a linear equation with a fitted intercept is more appropriate. In the selected alloy, regression produced R² = 0.937, and a constrained fit was σys = 0.383HV − 101.5 (with hardness and strength units consistent with the paper). Literature data for A356, A357, AA6061, and AA6063 also showed good linear Vickers-hardness/yield-strength relationships, although prior Brinell correlations for A356/A357 exhibited significant scatter. Important limitations are that the constraint factor depends on indenter geometry and material behavior, the zero-intercept Tabor assumption may fail, and aging state, strain hardening, precipitate evolution, and experimental or literature differences affect the correlation. The excerpt provides no direct evidence for Rockwell or nanoindentation-based predictions.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses Vickers-hardness/yield-strength correlations for an age-hardenable Al-Mg-Si alloy, but it does not provide comparative evidence for Rockwell, Brinell, or nanoindentation. The study solution-treated and artificially aged Al-0.5Mg-0.4Si specimens over 100–250 °C and 0.083–1000 h, measuring Vickers hardness and tensile yield strength. It presents the work as an experimentally based assessment of whether a hardness–yield-strength relation can be established and reports that comparable open-literature data were also reviewed. The relevant Tabor framework relates mean contact pressure (Mayer hardness, Pm) under an indenter to the material’s flow stress (σf) through a constraint factor, C; in conventional form this is Pm = Cσf (or σf = Pm/C). Thus, hardness can serve as a practical, semi-destructive proxy, but the relationship is empirical and material- and condition-dependent rather than universal. The excerpt specifically identifies dislocation accumulation during indentation as a cause of deviation from Tabor’s equation. Other limitations evident here are the need for calibration against tensile data and the fact that hardness measures indentation resistance while yield strength depends on deformation behavior, strain distribution, and alloy condition. The supplied pages do not quantify prediction error or establish performance across the four named hardness methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates hardness–yield-strength prediction primarily for Vickers hardness (HV) in age-hardenable Al–Mg–Si alloys; it does not provide comparable evidence for Rockwell, Brinell, or nanoindentation. Linear regressions vary substantially by alloy and dataset. Reported R² values range from 0.767 to 0.991, indicating that hardness can be a useful predictor within a consistent alloy, processing, and temper condition, but its accuracy is not universal. For the present alloy, the fitted relationship has a slope of 0.383 and a negative intercept of 101.5 (in the relevant stress/hardness units). Validation against experimental and literature data shows most predictions within 15%–30% error bands, while outliers involve differing solution treatments, quenching conditions, highly over-aged states, or differently homogenized samples. The Tabor framework relates flow stress to hardness; for fully work-hardened material, the excerpt gives σf = HV/(0.927C), with σf equated to yield strength. For strain-hardened materials, indentation produces a representative strain and σf exceeds σys, giving the modified relation σys = HV/(0.927C) − Δσ. Thus, the negative intercept reflects indentation-induced strain hardening. Correlations are limited by alloy chemistry, heat treatment, microstructure, strain-hardening behavior, and testing condition consistency.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that nanoindentation hardness can be compared with yield stress through an approximately linear empirical relationship, but it does not state a universal conversion constant or the Tabor relation. The authors compare nanohardness with both yield stress and tensile strength at multiple indentation depths, indicating that the quality of prediction depends on test depth and material condition. Nanoindentation hardness is nearly depth-independent above approximately 1 micrometer in many samples, whereas a strong indentation size effect appears at smaller depths; for example, ferritic-steel hardness rises substantially as depth decreases. This depth dependence would complicate using a single hardness-to-yield-strength conversion for aluminum alloys. The excerpt includes aluminum among the tested materials but gives no specific aluminum correlation or prediction error. Important limitations include pile-up and sink-in, which affect the estimated contact area; the Oliver–Pharr analysis used does not account for elastic–plastic effects; surface roughness and residual stresses may influence results; and crystallographic texture and anisotropy affect indentation modulus. The text also notes that hardness is less orientation-sensitive than indentation modulus, but polycrystalline heterogeneity can increase scatter. The cited study concerns nanoindentation rather than Rockwell, Vickers, or Brinell hardness, so it cannot establish how accurately those conventional scales predict aluminum-alloy yield strength.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes why hardness-to-yield-strength correlations—especially for nanoindentation—must be treated as empirical and conditional rather than universal. Nanoindentation hardness can be substantially overestimated at shallow depths because of the Indentation Size Effect (ISE): hardness increases as indentation depth decreases, particularly below approximately 10 μm. Thus, a hardness value depends strongly on test depth, indenter geometry, surface preparation, roughness, oxides or contamination, friction, and possible work-hardened surface layers. The article attributes size dependence partly to strain-gradient plasticity and geometrically necessary dislocations, whose contribution becomes important at submicron scales. This means nanoindentation hardness may not correspond directly to the bulk tensile yield strength measured in a conventional test. The study’s stated aim is to compare hardness measured at different depths with tensile properties and establish empirical relations, but the supplied pages do not provide the resulting equations, aluminum-specific correlations, or a Tabor relation. They also do not discuss Rockwell, Vickers, or Brinell correlations in detail. Consequently, this excerpt supports caution about interpreting hardness as yield strength, but cannot quantify how accurately each hardness method predicts aluminum-alloy yield strength or state the numerical Tabor coefficient.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide direct evidence for aluminum alloys, nor does it compare Rockwell, Vickers, Brinell, or nanoindentation hardness specifically against aluminum yield strength. Its results concern eutectic SnBi and relate hardness primarily to ultimate tensile strength (σUTS), so applicability to aluminum yield strength would require separate validation. The Tabor relation is represented here as a proportional relationship between Vickers hardness and ultimate tensile strength, with σUTS = HV/k (equivalently, HV = kσUTS), where k is the Tabor factor. For the investigated SnBi compositions, k was consistently above 3 and averaged approximately 4.0, although reported hardness and tensile-strength discrepancies produced ranges from about 3.3 to 5.2. Nanoindentation hardness was related to Vickers hardness through a multiplicity factor C1, approximately 1.7 (range 1.5–1.8). The excerpt emphasizes several limitations affecting hardness-strength correlations: different indentation techniques use different contact-area definitions; nanoindentation relies on projected area whereas conventional methods measure the imprint; pile-up, sink-in, elastic anisotropy, and related depth-to-area conversion errors introduce discrepancies; and microstructure, eutectic or second-phase strengthening, composition, and processing condition alter the coefficients. Consequently, coefficients should not be transferred automatically across materials or hardness methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the usual Tabor-style interpretation of hardness: in the fully plastic regime, mean contact pressure (or indentation hardness) is approximately a constraint factor of about 3 times the representative flow or yield stress. Thus, an estimated lower yield strength can be obtained by dividing the true mean contact pressure by approximately 3. In this aluminum alloy, the resulting nanoindentation lower-yield estimate was reasonably comparable to the bulk tensile 0.2% yield strength of about 0.32 GPa. However, the comparison is conditional rather than universal. Nanoindentation probes a localized volume and can show size-dependent strengthening, delayed plasticity, and abrupt pop-in; the pre-pop-in stress may be much higher than the bulk tensile yield strength. Hardness also reflects plastic flow and strain hardening, not necessarily a uniquely defined tensile yield point. If the alloy does not strain-harden, pile-up causes the standard contact-depth analysis to underestimate contact area and overestimate mean pressure; the excerpt notes errors of up to about 60% for pyramidal indenters and potentially more for spherical ones. Consequently, hardness-to-yield correlations depend on indenter geometry, constraint factor, contact-area calibration, pile-up/sink-in, strain-hardening behavior, microstructure, surface condition, and indentation size/length scale. The excerpt does not provide direct Rockwell, Vickers, or Brinell correlations, so its evidence is specifically for spherical nanoindentation of an aluminum alloy.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the specimen dimensions, estimated properties, or additive-manufacturing applications of small punch testing under ASTM E3205. It does, however, describe profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) as a method for extracting constitutive plasticity parameters and stress–strain behavior from an indentation test. PIP uses iterative finite-element simulations: parameters in a constitutive law are repeatedly adjusted until the simulated indent profile agrees optimally with the experimentally measured profile. The excerpt states that the Voce law is effective for representing the true stress–strain behavior of many metals. After the relationship is established, responses under other loading configurations—including uniaxial tensile testing—can be predicted. PIP offers approximately 1 mm spatial resolution, minimal sample-preparation requirements, and a combination of hardness-testing convenience with the more meaningful output of a tensile test. Automated systems can obtain stress–strain curves from a single indentation within a few minutes. The method has been applied or discussed for issues relevant to additively manufactured materials, including local property variations, residual stresses, exceptionally hard samples, weld regions, particulate metal-matrix composites, and anisotropy. The article specifically emphasizes that anisotropy is common or reported in LPBF maraging steels and that PIP has high sensitivity for detecting it. contexts.context: The excerpt describes alloy-screening approaches based on combinatorial materials libraries and automated microscale testing. Diffusion multiples create continuous composition gradients through interdiffusion; EMPA and scanning nanoindentation then map hardness and elastic modulus across ternary and binary composition regions. A single diffusion-multiple experiment can characterize an entire ternary system and produce multiple phase diagrams, whereas conventional one-by-one testing may require thousands of samples; the reported efficiency is roughly three orders of magnitude higher. Vapor-deposited graded Ti-Al films were similarly tested by nanoindentation to obtain mechanical properties as a function of composition. For residual stress, thin-film libraries were integrated on 7 × 7 micromachined cantilever arrays. Parallel laser-beam curvature measurement and CCD image processing enabled simultaneous curvature determination, after which Stoney’s formula yielded residual stress. The method achieved curvature resolutions of 5 × 10^-5 m^-1 for a silicon substrate or 10^-3 m^-1 for an individual cantilever, corresponding to 0.4 MPa stress resolution for a specified film/beam geometry, and was applied to Fe-Pd and Fe-Pt libraries. Automated scanning of microfabricated freestanding-film arrays also enables high-throughput bulge testing. The excerpt does not provide information about robotic test cells, miniaturized tensile arrays, small-punch testing, or their specific throughput rates and specimen counts.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports high-throughput automated nanoindentation as a rapid alloy-screening and property-mapping method, but it does not discuss robotic test cells, miniaturized tensile arrays, or small punch testing. Automated stage control and Accelerating Property Mapping (XPM) were used to generate dense hardness and modulus maps across heterogeneous materials, including welds, heat-affected zones, cladding/substrate interfaces, and multiphase steels. High-speed mapping can resolve local microstructural variations while also producing statistically meaningful distributions. One comparison used 196 nanoindentation grids with a 5-mN Berkovich indenter across a railway weld, occupying approximately the same area as a single Vickers test; the nanoindentation averages followed the conventional hardness trend but additionally captured scatter from heterogeneous microstructures. For homogeneous samples, arrays yielded n = 225 indents per specimen, about 20 times more tests than the n ≤ 10 common in many conventional nanoindentation studies. Operationally, reducing contact time from 20 seconds to 0.2 seconds reduced drift effects by two orders of magnitude and reduced tip wear, enabling many more tests per tip/sample combination. Thus, the excerpt indicates specimen-level counts from roughly 196–225 indents in demonstrated mapping/statistical experiments, but gives no absolute indents-per-hour rate.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses ASTM G34 exfoliation testing but does not provide the requested ASTM G47 or G139 stress-corrosion-cracking procedures, specimen dimensions, exposure temperatures, solution compositions, or test durations. It explains that exfoliation corrosion is an intergranular attack associated particularly with wrought aluminum alloys having elongated grain structures. Intergranular attack parallel to the surface produces hydrated aluminum oxide whose volume exceeds that of the original alloy, generating wedging stresses that lift surface grains and create the characteristic layered appearance. ASTM G34 (the EXCO test) assesses exfoliation susceptibility by exposing specimens to an oxidizing acidic chloride solution and comparing the resulting surface with standard photographs. The excerpt also mentions ASSET and MASTMAASIS tests, which use alternating salt-solution sprays and surface ratings. These tests are important for aerospace applications because exfoliation is a life-limiting airframe degradation mechanism: it removes load-bearing cross-sectional area and raises stresses in the remaining intact material, reducing mechanical properties. The passage therefore supports the purpose and significance of G34, but additional source material is required to specify G47/G139 testing and the exact G34 specimen and exposure requirements.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses ASTM G34 exfoliation testing, but it does not provide information on ASTM G47 or G139 stress-corrosion-cracking tests, including their specimen requirements, temperatures, solutions, or exposure durations. For G34, the EXCO immersion test evaluates exfoliation susceptibility in principally 2xxx and 7xxx aluminum alloys. It uses an aggressive solution containing 4.0 M NaCl, 0.5 M KNO3, and 0.1 M HNO3, initially at pH 0.4. Specimens are immersed continuously for approximately 48–96 hours, depending on alloy system, and the surface is visually rated from N (no appreciable attack) and P (pitting) through EA–ED degrees of exfoliation. The test can distinguish resistant and susceptible tempers, such as AA7075-T76 and AA7075-T6, and has correlated with atmospheric exposure for some alloys. However, it may overstate attack, fail to reproduce service environments, and correlate poorly for some Al-Li, AA2024, and 7x50 products. Modified EXCO solutions can improve correlation with actual service. These tests are important for aerospace aluminum because they identify susceptibility in lightweight, high-strength alloys before service, supporting temper selection, quality control, and prediction of durability in humid, salt-containing marine or industrial environments. The excerpt does not state specimen dimensions or temperature.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the ASTM G47, G139, or G34 specimen dimensions, exposure temperatures, solution compositions, or test durations. It does establish the mechanisms and significance that these standardized tests are intended to evaluate. Stress-corrosion-cracking tests reveal whether an aluminum alloy, under sustained tensile stress in a critical corrosive environment, initiates and propagates intergranular or transgranular cracks. SCC requires the simultaneous presence of a susceptible alloy, an aggressive environment, and tensile stress; crack initiation may occur at pits, surface discontinuities, or intergranular-corrosion sites. The discussion identifies anodic dissolution along active grain-boundary paths and hydrogen embrittlement as the two principal SCC propagation categories. Exfoliation testing evaluates susceptibility to layered, grain-boundary corrosion and material delamination; the excerpt specifically notes that IGSCC is one proposed mechanism of exfoliation corrosion. Microstructure is central: precipitate-free zones parallel to grain boundaries can be anodic and increase intergranular-corrosion susceptibility, while alloy particles and grain-boundary precipitates influence localized corrosion. These tests are important for aerospace aluminum because high-strength, age-hardenable alloys may retain adequate mechanical strength yet fail prematurely through localized corrosion, SCC, or exfoliation in service. Standardized exposures therefore support alloy, temper, heat-treatment, and maintenance qualification, although the cited excerpt alone cannot specify the ASTM procedures.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports the importance of surface roughness and build orientation for LPBF aluminum fatigue, but it does not provide data on porosity, hot-isostatic pressing (HIP), tensile strength, or numerical defect sizes. For Al2024-RAM2 produced by L-PBF, the tested orientations had roughness values of Ra = 2.1 µm (A-), 12.3 µm (B), 12.0 µm (C), and 17.6 µm (45°). Corresponding fatigue limits at 2 × 10^6 cycles were 118 MPa (A-), 115 MPa (C), approximately 115 MPa for B, and 109 MPa (45°). contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that fatigue performance of LPBF AlSi10Mg is strongly controlled by defect location, morphology, surface condition, and build orientation. Lack-of-fusion (LoF) pores are generally more damaging than spherical pores and are particularly detrimental in vertically built samples. In near-net-shaped, as-built, vibratory-polished, or jet-blasted specimens, fatigue cracks commonly initiate at surface pores; after milling, crack initiation shifts toward internal pores. Machining generally improves fatigue life by removing roughness, but it can expose previously subsurface pores, which then become crack-initiation sites. contexts.context: The excerpt describes profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) as an indentation method in which the surface profile produced by an indentation is measured after testing and interpreted using inverse finite-element modelling. FEM simulations of the indentation process are repeatedly run while the plasticity parameters in the constitutive law are varied until the simulated and experimental profiles agree optimally; this provides estimates related to the material stress–strain response, including yield and hardening behaviour. The excerpt does not specify the specimen dimensions, indenter-ball size, detailed profilometry procedure, or numerical accuracy for yield stress and work-hardening parameters, so those points cannot be established from this passage. Compared with conventional tensile testing, PIP requires minimal specimen preparation, avoids measurements during loading and concerns about loading-train compliance, and can obtain a stress–strain curve from a single indentation in roughly a couple of minutes. It also offers improved sensitivity to the stress–strain relationship, can identify in-plane anisotropy through asymmetry in the residual profile, and permits measurements at multiple indentation depths. Its ability to map local properties over approximately millimetre-scale surface regions is especially relevant to additively manufactured metals, where spatially varying properties and anisotropy are important; however, additive manufacturing is not explicitly discussed in this excerpt.

Its core workflow is iterative inverse finite-element modelling: plasticity parameters in a constitutive law are repeatedly adjusted until the simulated indentation response agrees optimally with experimental measurements. The article emphasizes that using the residual indentation profile—the three-dimensional topography of the indent—provides major advantages over relying only on the load–displacement curve and improves the reliability of converting indentation data into stress–strain curves. In the weld study, PIP detected slight anisotropy and mapped property changes across weld/parent-metal transition zones with approximately 1–2 mm lateral resolution, a scale difficult to examine using conventional tests. The reported PIP curves showed excellent agreement with conventional uniaxial tensile and compressive testing. contexts.context: Profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) extracts a bulk true stress–true strain curve from a spherical indentation. A ball is pressed into the specimen to a selected depth, the three-dimensional residual indent profile is measured by profilometry, and an inverse finite-element procedure iteratively adjusts the constitutive stress–strain curve until the simulated and measured profiles agree. For very hard metals, the indenter must remain elastic; silicon-nitride balls can be used, with proof-testing proposed to verify that a particular ball survives the full service range. Bulk measurements require a sufficiently large, representative many-grained volume rather than a nanoscale indentation, typically using a 0.5–1 mm ball and kilonewton-capable loading frame. The excerpt reports systematic agreement with tensile and compressive tests and describes the resulting curves as reliable, including for hard metals. It specifically highlights PIP’s usefulness at relatively high strains (about 15%) and its simpler implementation compared with uniaxial testing. The excerpt does not provide numerical accuracy values for yield stress or work-hardening parameters. It indicates applicability to thin plasma-sprayed layers and anisotropic additively manufactured materials, suggesting an advantage where conventional tensile specimens are difficult to produce, but does not quantify AM-specific accuracy or benefits.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) as an indentation method that extracts bulk stress–strain behavior through inverse finite-element modeling. A relatively large spherical indenter plastically deforms a region roughly hundreds of microns across, rather than the micron-scale volume affected in nanoindentation. After indentation, the residual surface profile is measured by profilometry. The measured profile is then compared with profiles predicted by FEM simulations, while constitutive-law parameters are iteratively varied until the modeled and experimental profiles agree optimally; the best-fit parameters provide the inferred plasticity response. The study uses a Voce constitutive law, with yield stress, saturation stress, and characteristic strain as the main plasticity parameters. Elastic constants are also required, but the outcome is reported to have low sensitivity to them, requiring only approximately 10–15% accuracy. The approach is intended to obtain representative properties of particulate metal-matrix composites when particles are relatively small (up to a few tens of microns) and homogeneously distributed. The excerpt does not provide quantitative accuracy for yield stress or work hardening, a direct comparison with tensile testing, the ball diameter, or specific advantages for additively manufactured metals. It does note that residual-profile fitting has important advantages over relying only on load–displacement data.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies PIP (profilometry-based indentation plastometry) as an indentation method capable of inferring a material stress–strain curve from a single experiment in roughly a couple of minutes. It states that PIP-derived curves generally agree very well with conventional tensile-test results, but the method relies on the true stress–true plastic strain relationship being representable by an analytical constitutive law. Consequently, unusual constitutive behavior—such as load drops and initial plastic bursts caused by dislocation escape from solute pinning atmospheres, or sigmoidal hardening from plasticity-induced phase transformations—may not be captured readily without specialized laws. PIP also cannot capture premature fracture occurring before necking or yielding and is therefore unsuitable for highly brittle materials when failure behavior is the focus. The excerpt mentions prior coarse-scale spherical indentation studies of welds, including Automated Ball Indentation, which uses a progressively increasing load applied through a hard sphere (typically a 0.3–0.8 mm radius cermet ball) with periodic partial unloading. However, this passage does not provide the requested details on PIP specimen dimensions, profilometry measurements, inverse finite-element modeling, quantitative yield-stress or work-hardening accuracy, or specific advantages for additively manufactured metals.

contexts.context: The excerpt introduces profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP) as a recently developed method for obtaining mechanical-property information from additively manufactured metals, particularly laser powder bed fusion maraging steel. It states that PIP generates stress–strain curves that can be compared with those from conventional uniaxial tensile and compression testing, and that PIP can detect anisotropy with high sensitivity. In this study, PIP results were consistent with systematic compression tests and electron backscattered diffraction: the material showed no significant anisotropy or crystallographic texture, despite tensile tests suggesting that the horizontal direction was harder than the vertical direction. The authors interpret the tensile difference as likely arising from strength variations caused by changing growth conditions at different distances from the build plate—in other words, inhomogeneity rather than true directional anisotropy. The excerpt does not provide the requested operational details of PIP, such as specimen dimensions, indenter-ball size, profilometry procedure, inverse finite-element-method formulation, quantitative accuracy for yield stress or work-hardening behavior, or detailed comparisons of advantages over tensile testing. It only indicates that PIP is advantageous for studying AM components and is sensitive to spatially varying properties.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes PIP as an inverse-FEM method based on spherical indentation. A measured indent is compared with FEM-predicted indent profiles, and the plasticity parameters in a constitutive law are varied until the predicted and experimental profiles agree optimally; this yields an inferred local stress–strain curve. The method probes a volume large enough to provide representative bulk properties while still permitting measurements in relatively small regions, making it suitable for mapping property gradients such as those produced by carburization. In the reported case-hardened steel study, the characterized layer was approximately 200 μm thick, while the hardened case extended to just over 1 mm. The excerpt states that carburization increased peak yield stress from about 1000 to 1400 MPa and produced substantial work hardening, and that the derived relationships were supported by comparisons between experimental Vickers hardness results and FEM predictions. Compared with conventional uniaxial tensile testing, PIP requires less specimen preparation and offers finer spatial mapping, whereas uniaxial testing has inadequate spatial resolution for shallow hardened layers. The passage does not provide specific indenter-ball dimensions, specimen-size limits, numerical accuracy/error bounds for yield stress or work hardening, or evidence concerning additive-manufactured metals. It only notes that PIP has previously been applied to mapping properties in fusion welds.

contexts.context: Vecchio’s HT-READ methodology is an integrated, closed-loop framework intended to accelerate bulk-alloy discovery by connecting computational screening, sample fabrication, processing, characterization, testing, and data analysis. Computational tools, including CALPHAD and machine-learning models, recommend candidate compositions. Those candidates are fabricated as a persistent, uniquely identified sample library rather than as isolated specimens. The demonstrated library uses 16 discrete samples arranged in a rotationally symmetric ring within a single 32 mm metallurgical mount. This geometry is designed to support automated positioning and multiple characterization techniques, including XRD, SEM/EDS, and EBSD, while preserving the ability to evaluate individual compositions. Experimental results are analyzed with artificial intelligence to identify composition–property relationships, and new data are fed into later screening and design iterations. The excerpt emphasizes that comprehensive microstructural characterization is the major rate-limiting step and that automation, miniaturization, parallelization, and rotational sample positioning are central solutions. It does describe a related automated high-throughput process–structure–property workflow for a γ/γ′ superalloy. A temperature-gradient furnace applies a continuous range of aging temperatures along one sample, after which nanoindentation and SEM measurements are taken at corresponding positions. Automated nanoindentation mapping uses automatic indent detection and scanning based on Angular selective Backscatter FE-SEM analysis, avoiding the slower conventional reliance on atomic force microscopy for topographic data. Mechanical properties are obtained through nanoindentation inverse analysis, combining instrumented indentation and pile-up analysis to calculate stress–strain curves. Automated FE-SEM image analysis determines precipitate fraction, size, and shape distributions. The reported output is 2,400 data points in 13 days, estimated to be approximately 200 times faster than conventional tensile-specimen methods, with the full dataset generated from a single sample. These results provide a comparable high-throughput nanoindentation and gradient-processing benchmark, but the supplied pages contain no evidence about HT-READ, small punch testing, or miniaturized tensile arrays.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines MMPDS-style statistical allowables rather than prescribing a universal specimen count. An A-basis allowable (T99) is a lower tolerance bound that at least 99% of the population is expected to meet or exceed, with 95% confidence. A B-basis allowable (T90) similarly requires at least 90% of the population to meet or exceed the value, also with 95% confidence. Allowables are calculated from the sample mean, standard deviation, and a derating/tolerance factor; that factor depends on the assumed distribution, sample size (degrees of freedom), desired coverage, and confidence level. The excerpt illustrates calculations using samples of 100, but this is an example, not a stated MMPDS minimum. For additive manufacturing qualification, the same statistical logic applies: specimens must represent the relevant material/process population, including expected variability across builds, locations, orientations, lots, and environments, and the test plan must support the selected basis and confidence. The appropriate number of specimens therefore depends on the governing MMPDS procedure, distributional assumptions, test design, and required reliability; it cannot be determined from this excerpt alone. A-basis is generally expected for nonredundant primary structural applications, while B-basis may be acceptable for redundant structures, subject to program and regulatory requirements.

It does explain why additive manufacturing qualification may require an alternative to a conventional, full-scale MMPDS-style allowables program. For friction stir welding, NASA used a phased strategy: an initial design-of-experiments sensitivity study defined process limits and a nominal process schedule; Phase I generated preliminary properties; Phase II added testing, process-specific data, and statistical comparisons; and Phase III compared certification panels, confidence panels, and a full-scale pathfinder article with the established database. This approach produced characteristic design values for specific material, thickness, joint configuration, tooling, and temperature—including cryogenic conditions. The report identifies cost and the rapid evolution of additive manufacturing as obstacles to a traditional allowables program. It therefore presents the FSW approach as an analogy for additive manufacturing and suggests a phased, efficient qualification strategy that can generate the test population needed for characteristic design values while allowing process development, materials characterization, analysis correlation, and certification to proceed in parallel. Because additive manufacturing products and process variables are highly customized, qualification must account for variables such as powder characteristics, power, scan speed, deposition pattern, layer thickness, atmosphere, thermal history, and build-plate position.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the numerical specimen counts or formal MMPDS definitions for A-basis and B-basis allowables. It does, however, explain how allowable values are adapted for additive manufacturing qualification. AM design values require an approach different from conventional metallic materials because each machine and process can introduce significant variability. Relevant sources include feedstock lot variability and reuse, build-to-build and machine-to-machine variation, coupon-to-part transferability, anisotropy, surface finish, thin walls, and build-history effects. Design values should be statistically substantiated using all appropriate data in the Material Property Suite repository, while including applicable variability and potentially additional safety margin. Qualification is not a one-time statistical exercise: design values must be continuously substantiated through process qualification, witness testing, integration with existing material data, and pre-production article evaluations. A machine-specific Process Control Reference Distribution statistically characterizes nominal witness-coupon behavior and is used to establish witness-test acceptance criteria. Engineering equivalence evaluates whether material remains in-family with baseline data by considering interconnected process, structure, property, and performance relationships rather than strength alone. Thus, MMPDS A- and B-basis requirements would need to be demonstrated with representative, statistically adequate AM data and confidence levels, while the AM qualification framework also verifies process stability and machine-specific control.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that MMPDS provides statistically guaranteed minimum material properties rather than relying on typical values. For conventional metals, A-basis and B-basis are the established allowables. For additive manufacturing, equivalent terminology is used because AM properties vary with build direction, build-plate location, machine, and software version: C-basis is the AM equivalent of A-basis, while D-basis is the equivalent of B-basis. The stated requirements are that C-basis is a minimum value exceeded by at least 99% of the population with 95% confidence, whereas D-basis is exceeded by at least 90% with 95% confidence. The excerpt does not provide a fixed specimen count for either allowable. It emphasizes that establishing a C-basis for one AM material–process combination may require testing hundreds of coupons across multiple machines and build batches. Thus, AM qualification must account for process and configuration variability rather than treating one dataset as universally applicable. The large physical-testing burden motivates validated physics-informed and computational models, including virtual coupon testing, to predict properties and reduce the number of required specimens while retaining statistically defensible qualification.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes MMPDS-style A- and B-basis allowables for additive-manufactured materials. An A-basis allowable is a conservative design value for which at least 99% of the material-strength population is expected to meet or exceed the value, with 95% confidence. A B-basis allowable requires 90% of the population to meet or exceed the value; the excerpt does not explicitly repeat the 95% confidence statement for B-basis, although the question supplies that criterion. B-basis values are intended for redundant structures in which failure of one element permits safe load redistribution. For full A- or B-basis determination, the cited plan calls for 100 tensile specimens drawn from 10 heats and 10 lots. If tensile allowables have already been established, only 20 specimens are needed for properties such as shear and compression allowables. A reduced B-basis plan uses 20 samples from three heats and reduced lots. For additive-manufacturing qualification, the process should establish a generic acceptance region across different batches, machines, and process conditions, then use it for qualification, proto-qualification, acceptance, and validation. Qualification may rely on extensive testing, reduced/equivalence-based testing, or model-based simulation. The described model-based approach combines material statistics, probabilistic analysis, Bayesian methods, and multiscale progressive-failure analysis to generate virtual specimens and reduce physical testing.
